speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CAPE BRETON-ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROJECTS TO PROVIDE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I should like to make an announcement relating to certain initial steps being taken by the government to help in providing alternative employment for persons affected by the closing of certain mines in Cape Breton. My colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys announced on May 30 that parliament would be asked to provide an amount of $1.5 million which would be set aside for approved projects for this purpose this year.
Two of the specific projects for which parliament will be asked to provide, I now wish to bring to the attention of the house. The first is a program of the Minister of Forestry for the improvement of forest stands in the area. This project offers a constructive means of improving the forest resource while simultaneously helping to meet the urgent problem of employment in Cape Breton. The total cost of this program during 1961-62 is estimated at $350,000, and it will provide employment for about 100 persons. It will be proceeded with immediately and the government of Nova Scotia will share in the cost.
Second, the government proposes to proceed immediately with the first stages of a program for the restoration of Louisbourg fortress as a tourist attraction. This was recommended by the Rand commission on coal. This project will also offer a most dramatic means of teaching the nation's history to its citizens and visitors. There are several alternative plans for the development of Louisbourg, and while a final decision has not yet been made among them, the preliminary work to be done this year, is common to all the alternative schemes. This work would involve preliminary surveys, installation of utilities, construction of various buildings for the work compound, rock quarrying and other items. The expenditure during this fiscal year
under this initial program at Louisbourg is estimated at $1,100,000, and it will provide employment this summer and next winter for an average of 145 persons.
A number of other projects, which, in the ordinary course of events would have formed part of the regular programs of various departments, are being accelerated. Taken together, these will provide a further 280 jobs in 1961-62. The entire program will involve an expenditure over several years of some $15 million. In addition, several other possible projects are under active investigation, and where necessary provision for these projects has been made in the supplementary estimates recently tabled.
The national employment service will be taking special steps, as various projects begin, to make certain that information regarding them is made available to persons displaced from employment in the coal mines of Cape Breton island.

subtopic: CAPE BRETON-ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROJECTS TO PROVIDE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word on the announcement which has just been made by the Prime Minister. He has announced two specific projects, one of which is for the improvement of forest lands. The Prime Minister did not say how near these lands were to the areas affected by the recent closure of one mine and the prospective closure on July 2 of the Florence mine; nor did he say whether it was the intention of the government to give preference in this employment to the miners. I would assume that would be the case because the fund, if
1	remember the original statement, was specifically for the purpose of providing employment for displaced miners.
The second project for the restoration of Louisbourg will, of course, involve considerable travel problems for any displaced miners because of the considerable distance Louisbourg is from the area in which mine closures have occurred. As I am sure the Prime Minister knows, because I imagine he has received a letter from the united mine workers of which I have a copy here, the workers at the Florence mine which is to close on July
2	are very concerned about the possibility of getting any alternative employment in that area so they can remain at their homes.
While what the Prime Minister has announced will be very far indeed from meeting the whole problem, it is an instalment which I am sure will be welcome.

Inquiries of the Ministry Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West): Mr. Speaker, this group is very pleased to hear of any proposal to provide employment for a few of the many Canadians at present unemployed.

speechtext: The hon. member for Skeena raised a question of privilege on June 7. I have given some thought to it. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HOWARD  STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
As the hon. member has a motion in mind, I think I should explain my views on the point.
On June 7 the hon. member tor Skeena alleged that the government had given incorrect information in a return to an order of the House of Commons made November 30, 1960, and alleged that this was a breach of the privileges of the house. I have the return, which is sessional paper No. 216A tabled by the Secretary of State on May 5, 1961. The questions ordered for return were as follows:
1.	Did any member of the cabinet Incur any travelling expenses between September 1, 1960 and October 31, 1960 Inclusive?
2.	If so, for each member of the cabinet what was, for each day, the amount of expense incurred, the place travelled to and the purpose of the visit.
The return made to that order of the house was as follows:
There is no official record from which the information called for by this order of the house can be drawn. Under a well established practice, expenses incurred by cabinet ministers when travelling on official business are paid out of departmental administration or other appropriate votes without any accounting being required therefor, irrespective of whether or not an advance is made.
In support of his allegation the hon. member put forward question No. 381, asked by the hon. member for St. Denis and answered orally by the Postmaster General on June 7, as reported at page 5965 of Hansard. I do not think I shall take time to read it. Hon. members will find the question and the answer at this page. There the Postmaster General gave particulars of some of his recent travel expenses. The other relevant fact was the assertion by the Minister of Finance at page 5966 that the answer given to the order for return was a correct one and in accordance with the practice of the house.
The problem presented to me was whether the complaint of the hon. member for Skeena, which he is undoubtedly entitled to make at one time or another, was properly made as a question of privilege at the time it was made. If a question of privilege of the house is involved, the rules permit it to be brought before the house at once. If it is not a question of privilege the hon. member would have to wait for an appropriate opportunity to bring the matter before the house, for example as a grievance upon a motion to go into supply, upon the estimates of any department which make money available for travelling expenses of ministers, or by the usual notice of motion which at this stage of the session is not a very practicable remedy.
I do not propose to take time to review the authorities on the nature of parliamentary privilege, but I refer hon. members to May's
IMr. Howard.]
Parliamentary Practice, sixteenth edition, pages 42 and 43; Bourinot's Parliamentary Practice, fourth edition, page 37 and to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, page 93 and following. There it is indicated that protection against outside interference by the crown, by the courts, by the House of Lords and other outside influences was the origin of privilege. In our house I find no instance where a return of information to an order of the house has been attacked as a matter of privilege on the ground that the return was inaccurate, unduly delayed, or otherwise unsatisfactory as a compliance with an order of the house.
In the report of debates for 1895, at pages 1830 to 1842, there is an interesting precedent, where a complaint was made that the government had failed for more than two years to bring forward a return of information in response to an order of the house. The house was asked to give leave for an hon. member to move the adjournment, as would now be done under standing order 26, to discuss the matter. I shall take a moment to refer to this precedent. At page 1830 of the debates of 1895 the member for Both-well said:
Before the Clerk calls the orders of the day, I desire to call the attention of the government and of the house to what seems to me to be a contempt of the rules and rights of the house; and, if it is necessary to a discussion of this subject that I should move the adjournment of the house, I make that motion. More than two years ago, I moved, in this house, for a return, and I stated that my reason for that motion-
Then he went on to say:
The whole of that session went by without that return being brought down.
The succeeding session went by; he was then in the third session when he brought the matter forward in this way. There was a lengthy discussion of the position. I would just like to refer to what Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Speaker said at page 1839:
It is a breach of duty on the part of the government; and though my hon. friend from Bothwell took an extreme course in bringing this matter before the house by moving the adjournment, still he was within his right. Let me quote the opinion of Dr. Bourinot on this subject:
"Every care should be taken by the department or officer whose duty it is to furnish the return, to have it strictly in accord with the terms of the address or order. If a person neglects to furnish a return or frames it so as to mislead the house, it will be considered a breach of privilege, and he will be reprimanded or more severely punished, according to the circumstances of the case."
At the same page, Mr. Speaker said:
Before putting this question, I desire again to express my opinion with regard to the inconvenience of this mode of bringing up a discussion. I am, of course, in the judgment of the house in dealing with this matter, but I may point out that there are other ways in which a question of

this kind might be raised without moving the adjournment of the house. In the first place, a motion might be put upon the paper censuring the government. Then there is another way in which the matter might be brought up without any notice at all, that is, on going into committee of supply.
Then he quoted Sir Erskine May. The Speaker then concluded as follows:
That, to my mind, is conclusive that a question of this kind for the redress of a grievance, should more properly be discussed on moving the house into committee of supply.
He treated the matter as one of grievance.
Although I cannot find that it has been done before, it is possible that an open and obvious defiance of an order of the house might be raised as a breach of privilege in the nature of contempt of the authority of the house. Such situation, if it arose would seem to me to go deeper than the privileges of the house, which are ancillary procedures in support of its authority, and would seem to involve a question of the confidence of the house in the government.
In the present case there is no obvious disrespect by the government of the order of the house. The order has been complied with, and the answer was available to the hon. member some time ago. There may be some inconsistency between the return and the oral answer, but as I said hon. members have other means of challenging such inconsistencies without the use of a superseding privilege motion.
In the circumstances, which include an interval of delay in objecting to the return, I do not think the hon. member would be warranted in asking to introduce a motion based on privilege.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday during the discussion of the minister's estimates I had the opportunity to discuss a seven year plan or program involving projects in which the federal government has an interest. I had the opportunity to deal with the proposed breakwater at the most advantageous place on the south side of English bay in my riding. I also had the opportunity of discussing a plan of proper development of the False creek area, which I hope in the future will be renamed either Kitsilano harbour or Kit-silano bay.

Supply-Public Works
This morning I should like to discuss for a few minutes another matter in which the federal government has an interest. I refer to the major defence installations in the Jericho beach area. Before the war we had at Jericho beach a very fine golf course known as the Jericho golf and country club. This course added considerable beauty to the city and was cherished by golfers and nongolfers alike. Then the war came along and the air force and army took over the property. Wooden barrack-type buildings were erected, and along the waterfront air force hangars were constructed. These buildings have been there now for many years, and the people in the community are anxious to see them vacated.
During the war no one took serious objection to buildings of that type, but as the war is long since over the citizens of Vancouver would like to see a major renovation of the entire area. I suggest that there would be many advantages to the city and to the defence department should the army and air force units be withdrawn entirely from the Jericho and Kitsilano areas. Withdrawal of these units from the city and thus from the waterfront area would allow for that type of city development which, as I have stated, the citizens have long desired.
From the sale of these lands at Jericho beach the defence department could build at Surrey, let us say, a new and modern installation which would satisfy the requirements of the defence department and would certainly permit the city officials to plan the proper development of the Jericho area. The benefits all round would be enormous. In making these suggestions I am not unmindful of what has been done in such cities as London, Berlin and Cologne since the war.
Vancouver, as everyone knows, was never touched by the ravages of war, yet it seems to take us longer to remove the flotsam and jetsam of war buildings than other cities which received terrible punishment. I must emphasize that Vancouver gave up the Jericho and Kitsilano areas in order to prosecute the war, but we need these areas once more in order to set up a reserve of green spaces. I believe the records will show that in 1943 the federal government purchased 7.8 acres of the Jericho golf and country club for the very nominal sum of $55,000. The senior government also acquired 140 additional acres in this area from the province of British Columbia. One of the major issues in Vancouver at the present time is the acquiring of further green areas for park development. One isue at the present time is whether or not another area known as the Shaughnessy golf club should be purchased

for park purposes in the city of Vancouver, but the holdings of the army and air force are almost forgotten.
The armed forces occupy 192 acres of prime land along the Jericho and Kitsilano waterfront. My question is, is it necessary for these twin military establishments to be where they are? Is the military community a multimillion dollar white elephant or a multimillion dollar necessity? These two establishments employ a total of 488 officers and men, which works out to 2.5 men per acre. In addition there are 377 civilian employees of the Department of National Defence.
The removal of the defence installation would provide us with a major public works project in the Vancouver area. It certainly would do so if the military forces vacated. The Minister of Public Works would no doubt be able then to call for the sale of the land and a proper housing and park development could take place there. Therefore I urge the minister to give very serious consideration to the proper development of that area.
As I mentioned yesterday, the defence department occupies a major holding near the south end of Burrard bridge, and if the defence department vacated that area and the Jericho area a major military construction project could be undertaken say in Surrey, which would be carried out by the minister's department. A major establishment could be set up there which would certainly please the military forces. These two important areas in or near Burrard riding are two major issues, and I hope progress can be made at an early date.
I also hope the Minister of Public Works will give consideration to the resolution passed by the city of Vancouver in 1941 which allowed one of the government departments to enter that area upon the condition that they would vacate it at the cessation of hostilities. The war is long since over but these installations are still there, and I hope the present administration will comply with the terms upon which the particular department entered that area.
I noticed in the paper last night that the national capital commission is planning a cultural centre in mid-town Ottawa, on the east bank of the Rideau canal. The newspaper article says that the cultural centre will likely contain a convention hall or auditorium, and perhaps a theatre to start. The project is to rise on 22 acres near the Union station. The newspaper article went on to say that the Prime Minister had suggested that centennial planning for the capital might cover such things as a convention hall-auditorium, a national theatre and even a stadium or arena.

This is a wonderful development for this area, and I am not necessarily criticizing it. I also noticed a photograph with relation to a major development at Niagara Falls. The newspaper article says that a multi-million dollar permanent international cultural trade exposition at Niagara Falls has been approved by Ottawa. We also learned from the newspapers earlier and heard in the house that the federal government was prepared to advance to the city of Montreal and to Quebec some $40 million to hold a world's fair in 1967 in Montreal. We are also aware of the fact that at Dawson Creek, a rather small community in the interior of British Columbia, the federal government is advancing a considerable sum of money for the restoration of a theatre in order that the community may celebrate the centennial in 1967. Other cities are planning major projects.
The point I want to make is that Vancouver is likewise in great need of an allpurpose auditorium. We feel that if this type of development can take place in eastern Canada, then by the same argument we should also be able to proceed with such a development in the west. Vancouver is a long way from Ottawa, and I think we can make a special case for the fact that we need a similar building on the west coast. We are in the Pacific trade theatre, and this type of building would help us very much in the field of trade and commerce. As the minister knows, we need a coliseum very badly, and I hope he will give consideration to assisting us with the construction of an all-purpose coliseum in the Vancouver area.
There are numerous advantages to this project. The trade and commerce field will certainly benefit, as will the tourist industry. This proposed building could be used as one of the main buildings for the Pacific exposition, if we are able to proceed with our plans for it in 1967. I think we can make a special case for Vancouver in this regard. Since this is my only request at this moment, I hope the minister will be able to make available to us one of his fine architects who could design us a building in which the C.B.C. could be housed as well as the coliseum. In Boston, the Boston Gardens is built over the top of the Union station.
I understand that the C.B.C. is in great need of storage accommodation for their many properties. If we need a coliseum and the C.B.C. need a building for their properties, surely with proper planning we could design a building to accommodate our coliseum and give the federal government room for the C.B.C. My request in this regard is that the minister try to assist us in constructing an 90205-6-409i

all-purpose coliseum on the plot of land already owned by the C.B.C.

I am sure the minister will be glad to learn that, unlike the hon. gentleman who just preceded me, I intend to keep my observations generally within the ambit of the Department of Public Works. I think everything the hon. gentleman mentioned concerned some other department than the Department of Public Works, that is so far as I was able to follow him. The minister will be pleased to learn also that I do not intend to be quite as harsh in my criticism of the present government as the hon. gentleman who just spoke. This does not mean that I will not have a few critical observations to make.
I join wholeheartedly in the criticism made yesterday by the hon. member for Churchill of the dilatory actions of this government, in which the hon. member was reflecting the views of the new provincial Liberal leader in Manitoba, in dealing with the problem of Churchill. The hon. gentleman ended his remarks by expressing a pious hope that something would be done. If the government moves in the matter of Churchill at the same speed that it has moved in respect of the Red river floodway, then I think the hon. member for Churchill's successor will be addressing another government about this matter before anything ever happens.
I should like also to join with the hon. member for St. John's East in his criticism of the government which appears on page 6422 of Hansard, and which I understand was exceptionally palatable to the minister. As reported on that page the hon. member said:
I should also like to bring to the attention of the minister at this time my sense of disappointment at the fact that the vote for Newfoundland under construction of public buildings is substantially smaller compared with other provinces of similar size. It is substantially smaller than the vote for Nova Scotia and substantially smaller than the vote for the province of New Brunswick.
This is true, sir. For the first couple of years this government was able to carry on the building projects and policy of expansion which the minister and his predecessor inherited from Mr. Winters. However, when they ran out of those plans that Mr. Winters had prepared, they had no program of their own so far as public construction in the city of St. John's was concerned. There is no evidence that any plans are being made.
I happen to know, of course, that it was the intention of the previous government, which did things and did not just talk about them, and which had a program of expansion which helped this country to grow as compared with the stagnation of the last four

Supply-Public Works
years, to phase this building program so there would be a reasonably continuous level of employment on public construction in St. John's. Moreover, there is a very strong argument which I have made many times before and which I intend to make again for structures outside of St. John's in some of the smaller places, particularly buildings to house the Post Office Department.
It just so happens, and the statistics have been put on the record many times, that in Newfoundland, unlike New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, there are practically no rural routes. The treasury is therefore saved the very considerable cost of free rural mail delivery which the other provinces do get. Perhaps for a long time to come, because of the nature of the settlements along the coast, Newfoundland will be less adaptable to that kind of thing. It is the custom there to go to the post office to get the mail. In Newfoundland, therefore, unlike the other provinces, the needs of the Post Office Department are quite different. In the first place, in practically all the smaller places the C.N.T. is in the post office, and that creates a different situation at once. The second thing is that in Newfoundland it is entirely unacceptable, for historical reasons, to have post offices in shops or stores or other places of business, which is the usual thing in the rural areas of the rest of Canada. There is, on the ground of laying out a reasonable amount of public funds to give comparable service, every reason why there should be some exception made in Newfoundland, and some exception has been made. I have expressed appreciation to this minister and his predecessor for continuing to replace public buildings in Newfoundland where they existed in the old days.
However, what the government will not do is to put a building in any place that did not have a building before confederation, notwithstanding the fact that some of these places have grown considerably larger than some of the places that do have public buildings. I refer, of course, to a community like Hare Bay, which received a good deal of notoriety only last week when the whole place was almost consumed by the great forest fire. While I have persisted in my advocacy of this policy over the years, and I have not yet had any success, I feel that if I keep on trying there is always a chance, particularly as we get nearer to an election, that the government might decide to do something about this or at least indicate that some day it might.
I do want to join with the hon. member for St. John's East in saying that I think St. John's should be better treated so far as a public building program is concerned. If this

government really meant what it said about having an expansionist policy, then St. John's would have been better treated. The fisheries department there needs a new building, as well as other departments that were referred to by the hon. member the other day.
What is even more distressing than the public building situation is the marine works situation in Newfoundland. After all, this work is even more vital to the economy and to the life of the people in the outports. It is true that if you look at the global figures for marine works in the estimates this year, they are up $300,000 over last year. They have not gone down very much as compared with earlier years. They have varied little from year to year. There is a high proportion of the money now being spent on the harbour development at St. John's, which of course was only started two years ago, though the plans were laid in 1956 and 1957. When you abstract the amount being spent on St. John's harbour you see that there has been a tremendous shrinkage in the marine works program in the province of Newfoundland compared with what it was in the first year the present government was in office, or in the year both governments were in office, or in previous years.
It is not as though there are not projects that urgently need to be done. There are plenty of projects. The minister knows this from correspondence he has had with me, and I think he will testify that I am an assiduous and patient correspondent and that nothing discourages me, even the minister's replies.
The minister will recognize that in one of the seven constituencies there are plenty of works which he and his officials have admitted are deserving of consideration-I have it in writing that he has said that they are deserving of consideration-and which are not getting done.
Moreover, Mr. Chairman, they are not getting done at a time when the rate of employment in Newfoundland is higher, unhappily, than the national average-indeed it is considerably higher than the national average -and when a redoubled effort should be made. These works are ones that have a fairly high labour content. They would employ a great many people. They would save the drain on welfare funds or on the unemployment insurance fund. There is everything to be said for getting them done, because they are all works that would add to the income of the community in which they would be situated, or practically all of them are of that type.
I just want to remind the minister of a few of them. I am not going into the details;

he has them all. The first place is Newman's Cove. I feel particularly badly about the situation at Newman's Cove, although I know very well what the difficulty is. Because of the exposed harbour there it is a difficult place in which to build a wharf that will stay put. Of course we do not want built a wharf that is going to be carried away by the ice. That is one of the most active fishing communities in the whole of Bonavista bay, at least, and certainly on the south side of the bay. A great deal of fish is shipped from that place. As a matter of fact there is a structure there now that takes up too much of the space of the present wharf. I would certainly put Newman's Cove at the top of any list I made of places that ought to be served. I feel a certain sense of responsibility-I was almost going to say guilt-about this place because by sheer inadvertence this wharf was not included previously. I may say that it was inadvertence-for which I do not think I have any direct responsibility, but I was a member of the government at the time-that it was not included in 1957, and it should have been included.
Then I wish the minister would have his officials take another look at the situation at Upper Amherst Cove. There is a slipway there, and it is another very difficult place. There are many fishermen there who would earn twice as much from the fishery and would catch twice as much fish if they had a wharf on which to land them. Then in view of the catch I think Plate Cove West ought to have an extension to its wharf. I plead for Plate Cove West, notwithstanding the fact that I did not do very well there myself in the last election and the minister's friend did much better than I did. Notwithstanding that fact, I commend Plate Cove West to the minister. Perhaps that particular commendation would appeal to him more than some others.
The next most important one after Newman's Cove in Bonavista south is Princeton. The minister has had a great deal of correspondence about Princeton, which is frightfully important for two reasons. It is one place where the railway touches the shore, and it is a transshipment point for freight carried on the railway all through the southern part of the bay. Princeton is also a considerable fishing place. There would be more fisheries and much more productive fisheries at Princeton if that wharf could be built. It is a very small structure that is needed, and it would not cost a great deal.
On the south side of Bonavista bay the one other place that really has been neglected is Sweet Bay. I think Sweet Bay gave me a majority once out of three times. Perhaps
Supply-Public Works
the minister would therefore think kindly of Sweet Bay. If everybody had treated me in the way Sweet Bay treated me, maybe I would not have been here. At any rate,, whatever the people of Sweet Bay may have-thought of me, I think a great deal of them and I think they should have a wharf.
Then there has been a recent request, and' this gives me a chance to say a word of commendation of the department. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, I do not mind saying a word of commendation of the department with regard to many things. However, I want to say a particular word of commendation of the department after I have mentioned this next project. I refer to Lethbridge. Lethbridge is not a fishing place, and I would' not pretend for one second that it was. I would never have asked for a wharf at Lethbridge. There is an old wharf where there is not enough water to get a good sized canoe alongside. That is not the fault of the government of Canada. That was one of the mistakes made by the commission of government. Lethbridge has not too much deep water. However, somewhere on that side of the bay, as opposed to the Musgrave-town side, a wharf is needed because a big pulpwood operation is going to be starting up in that area.
That brings me to my point of commendation. The government spent a large sum of money on an extremely long wharf-the longest one in my constituency and one of the most impressive-at Carmanville. I am sure the minister and his officials will be glad to learn that millions of cords of pulp-wood are being shipped over that wharf at the present time to Italy, bringing an income not only to that settlement but to the whole of that coast, and that dozens and perhaps hundreds of families have been kept from drawing unemployment insurance and have been kept off relief in this area because that wharf is there. It is certainly one of the best investments recently made by the government in expansion.
I am glad to say, of course, that the replacement was planned in the old days, but the government carried out those plans and carried them out very expeditiously, although it was a very big job and I am sure that at times they may have wondered whether it was going to be justified. I should like them to know that it has been amply justified, as would be these other projects, I am satisfied, if they were carried out. If the government want an expansion program, this is the kind of expansion from which they would get dividends. I am not suggesting the waste of public funds on useless wharfs.

Supply-Public Works Perhaps not quite so strong as the plea for Sweet bay, I would also plead for Winter-brook, which is not so much a fishing area generally but where there is a big lobster fishery. A small landing at Winterbrook would be helpful. I would also hope that the minister would take another look at Glovertown north. I should also like to have a careful look taken at the situation at Greenspond, the old capital of the north, on the north side of the bay. It is one of the most historic places in Newfoundland. Unhappily it is an island, and it is extremely hard for these islands to survive. It has the biggest population of any of the islands in Bonavista bay. Most of the rest of them are becoming depopulated. While I would not advocate any large expenditures at Greenspond, because it is a difficult place to get at, still it has a very lucrative fishery, and I should like to think that adequate facilities will be maintained there.
Going around Cape Freels and into Notre Dame bay I come first of all to Lumsden south. I was at Lumsden south one day in the fall in a very rough sea indeed. I saw men bringing in a boat on the rocks on the beach, and two of those men were all but killed; in fact I could hardly believe they would not be killed. It was the most marvellous manifestation of the skill for which Newfoundland seamen are famous that they were not killed, and all because we cannot get an extension to that slipway. In terms of dollars it is a very small project in this great fishing area, one of the most historic fishing areas of the whole of Newfoundland. We are not even asking for a wharf, just a slipway for pulling up the boats. This is desperately needed, particularly in the rough weather in the fall.
Then coming to Fogo island, the minister knows there is a modified proposal now for the development of Fogo harbour. I know it is a difficult problem; no one knows it better than I do, except perhaps the engineers of the department. There are 5,000 people on Fogo island and the town of Fogo is the centre of the island. They are all fishermen; there is no other industry at all. If the town of Fogo cannot have adequate marine facilities 5,000 people are going to be in a very desperate economic plight.
There is another place on Fogo island that deserves some consideration. That is Stag Harbour. They have a nice little wharf there but it is not big enough to handle the traffic. When the wharf was built the people moved off one of the islands just off Fogo island on to Fogo island, doubling the population there. They are fishing people; they are fishing all

the time, and they need adequate landing space and perhaps a little more depth of water.
Then I come to two places in Dog bay, Hor-wood and Stoneville. They had wharves in the past, but their wharves have gone. These unfortunate people are not fishermen; they are woods workers. They have to get away from there to work in the woods because the great mill that used to be there is not operating any longer. They have no way of getting out. The provincial roads program will get there eventually, but the provincial government is strapped for funds and it has so many claims for local roads. These people should have a wharf in at least one of those places. I would like to see wharves in both places. The minister could even flip a coin as far as I am concerned-and I do not mean any pun there-as to which place to put it, as long as he puts one there so the people will be able to get out and the coastal boats get in and land the people properly.
I think the minister ought to take another look at Port Albert and Boyd's Cove. The situations are very different. Port Albert will not get a road for quite a while; it is the other place besides Horwood that will not have a road for quite some time, I am afraid. But Port Albert in the wintertime, in the spring and fall is used by people coming from Change islands and Fogo island to get to the mainland of Newfoundland. It is a small place, but there are fishermen there and I think if we had a wharf we would increase the value of the fishery. In addition we would have certain other advantages accruing. I think in time this would become a big settlement, instead of a small settlement, through the moving in of people from the islands.
Boyd's Cove is a different kettle of fish. The road is being built to Boyd's Cove and will be through there this year. That normally would be regarded by the department as a reason for not building a wharf, but I suggest that Boyd's Cove is now going to become the main terminal for getting out to the islands in the spring and fall. Also, as the minister and his officials know, a causeway is going to be built across to New World island from Boyd's Cove and there will be a need not for an elaborate structure but for a wharf there to handle the traffic that can reasonably be expected.
The minister will be pleased to hear that I am coming to the end of my remarks. I could give the minister a lot more requests than these, but I am only picking out the urgent cases. There is Whale's Gulch. I still think the department could find enough ingenuity to do something for Whale's Gulch. I will not go into the problem because the

department knows it very well, and it is a tough one. These are wonderful people; they are all fishermen, and they should be able to get in and out of that place a little more easily and with a little less peril. I know about this because I went there on a rough day myself and our boat was nearly swamped trying to get in.
Then there is Bridgeport, the most important of all the fishing settlements of New World island. The minister's officials have told me-and this has always hurt my feelings because they should really have known better-that Bridgeport is only two miles from Moreton's Harbour by road. That is quite true, but it is not much comfort to a fisherman who in order to get to the wharf at Moreton's Harbour has to go all the way around Western Head. I went around Western Head in the election campaign of 1958, and I can tell the minister he would not like to have been with me that day. Bridgeport is a real fishing place-

speechtext: Just that day?

It was one day in March or February, 1958, and it was quite a day. At any rate, Bridgeport should have a wharf. It should have had a wharf some time ago. We should have built one there. We made a mistake in not building it, and I am asking the minister to correct that mistake. He can take all the credit he likes for correcting the mistake if he will build the wharf.
You made quite a few mistakes.

I wish the minister would look into the question of the dredging needs at Durrell's Arm, particularly, Upper Jenkins Cove. I had a telegram only the day before yesterday from the community council at Crow Head in Twillingate. The minister knows that one of these community stages was built there. No community stage has benefited a community more. There is a wonderful co-operative spirit in that place, and the people are using the stage to such an extent that the wharf just will not handle the traffic. They do need an extension to the wharf in order to carry on their business and in order to make it pay and really be useful. I think perhaps the minister could squeeze the small amount required for that project out of his miscellaneous vote, and he could not use it in any better way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask about something which is of great interest in my riding. We have a problem in the town of Haileybury. Without a doubt we are going to have to build a post office there, because the lease is up on the building
Supply-Public Works
now being occupied. It has become obsolete, and it is certainly not a satisfactory building for a post office.
I think as we will soon have to construct this building, this would be a good time for the department to consider the needs in that area for federal buildings. For a great many years there has been a legitimate complaint, in Kirkland lake, and it still exists, that a building should be built to house the federal departments in the area. One of the very grave problems for a long time has been the housing of the offices of the unemployment insurance commission. These offices have been located in rented premises. If this is possible, they are even more crowded than some of the offices in the House of Commons, and I think that is probably the height of overcrowding. These people have had to sit in the corridor and in front of the door with the wind blowing in at 60 miles an hour. The conditions which exist would certainly not pass the Ontario factory act, because there is terrific overcrowding.
At no time has the decision been finalized to construct a building in which to house these people. As the minister is aware, renovations are taking place in the federal building. The post office in Kirkland Lake is not going to be changed, but there will be a change to the upstairs part of the unemployment insurance property now housing the post office. This seems to be unsatisfactory, because it will be necessary to move the R.C.M.P. out or put them in less suitable quarters, and the reserve units of the army will have to be shifted around.
It seems we should have a survey which would take into consideration the needs of the federal departments for some time to come. That is why I am asking whether a survey of this type could not be carried out in the Haileybury area. I will arrange that a petition be circulated in Haileybury asking for a federal building to house the post office in that area, but I believe other things should be taken into consideration.
This is one of the reasons I have not pressed this matter in the past. It seems to me that the civil defence organization is bound to need some accommodation in this area, and probably this should be considered in connection with the arrangements made for the Algonquin regiment, which has its headquarters in Haileybury. The land presently owned is sufficient to allow a federal building to be built on it, though I do not suggest that it could not be built in a better situation. However, there is enough land there to serve as a site for the post office, a building which would take into consideration the needs, both present and future, of some of the other

Supply-Public Works
officials working in that area; for example, the staff engaged in carrying out the provisions of the Veterans' Land Act and the work of the Department of Veterans Affairs. There are also the inspectors and officials of the Department of Agriculture. The Department of Public Works has no representatives in the area, and the fact that officials have to be sent from North Bay undoubtedly interferes with the speedy handling of requests made from areas further north.
The situation could probably be dealt with better by setting up a permanent office in the area. The unemployment insurance commission has arranged that a branch will be established before the end of the year in New Liskeard. If this is so the officials will obviously have to be housed in a federal building, because rental accommodation in that area is limited. I am suggesting that the minister should survey the requirements of the whole area so that the town of Hailey-bury will be able to get a post office large enough to also house other federal agencies which can be located in the town, and that with the establishment of the new unemployment insurance office in New Liskeard consideration be given to housing in one building the other agencies which are now operating from buildings in adjacent areas.
I am not sure, Mr. Chairman, how we go about arranging these things and getting them done. I am not interested in this question in a political way. If it is necessary to bring the defeated Conservative candidate into the negotiations, if the department feels it is necessary to send him around, it is perfectly all right with me, because we both come from the same area; we both recognize the needs of that area and are sympathetic to them. If this is the way it should be done, I do not object to having some assistance. But I do believe that these projects should not be carried out by bits and pieces. I believe that while we are building premises in Hailey-bury to house the post office we should consider other demands which are likely to arise for accommodation. I suggest that the minister should give consideration to the needs of his colleagues who are concerned with civil defence and the desirablility of finding accommodation for civil defence staff in this area. As I say, this might be considered in close connection with the Algonquin regiment, whose history throughout northern Ontario is highly respected. The fact that the regiment has for many years had its headquarters in the town of Haileybury would indicate to me the desirability of having the civil defence headquarters for the northern region in that area also.

There is another problem and I am not sure what happens about it, but I am concerned with docks, wharves and other facilities on lake Timiskaming. For many years we have, without doubt, neglected lake Timiskaming. I am sympathetic toward the question raised by the hon. member for Hull when he speaks in this house about the forward looking program we should be developing in connection with the Ottawa river. This is only part of the problem, which affects the upper Ottawa river, which includes lake Timiskaming.
This whole area is now faced with all the problems of conservation which other areas faced earlier in their development. One of these is erosion. I have often heard members from the maritime provinces talking about erosion and the assistance which is given to combat it. I think some of this assistance should be available to lake Timiskaming, which is an interprovincial body of water. I see that the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister is in his seat. His riding covers all the other side of those waters, and he will agree with me, I hope, that the survey which appears to me to be necessary should not be made on a partisan basis. It should not even be on an exclusively provincial-federal basis. It should be on a scale sufficiently large to include both the conservation authorities and the municipalities.
Obviously control dams will be needed in the riding of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue. They will be needed on the White river and on the Quinze river as well as on the Wabi, on the Moose, the Matache-wan and on the Montreal river. Each of these rivers will need control dams, and these dams will have to compensate for the abuses which are taking place at the present time in connection with the use of the water by Ontario hydro. Ontario hydro does not give one hoot to what happens to the Ottawa river or to the Ottawa river watershed. They could not care less what happens to it. All they are interested in is getting a head of water to produce a certain amount of electricity.
Last year, on one occasion when I went home, I found that my area was flooded. The town of New Liskeard had water in its streets. I am sure the hon. member whose constituency lies across the lake found exactly the same situation in all the towns along the lake shore on his side. When one is asked to make representations asking that water be let out at the south control dam, one is well aware at the time that both at Britannia, here, and all the way up the Ottawa river other places are flooded also. This is a situation which should not exist, and it would not

exist were it not for the inability of the hydro authorities to look at this problem in a larger light than that of their own interests, which, as I say, consists of maintaining a head of water for the generation of electricity.
I do not know whether this question can be settled now. I do not even know whether the government has any interest in making a survey of the whole situation in the Ottawa watershed, but this is an important matter. Within the next few years it will arise internationally, and we shall be obliged to give consideration to a project which will be as important to the Canadian people as is, presently, the problem associated with the Columbia river agreement. The same situation will arise in relation to the need which has already developed in Chicago, where there is not even enough water to meet the sewage disposal needs in that area. And, of course, the only place from which we can get water is the Ottawa river watershed, supplemented, of course, by water taken from the Arctic watershed.
I am not asking the federal government to make that survey now, because it still seems unrealistic to me. I am not really suggesting to the minister that we survey the Ottawa river with the object of putting in a canal. This seems kind of unrealistic to me as well. The only reason it sounds unrealistic to me is that I am not an engineer and I am not really a conservation expert, and I do not know what the potentials and possibilities are; but many people much smarter than I have said that it a feasible project, and both these things will come to pass at some time in the future. I think we would be foolish not to take these problems into consideration.
Lake Timiskaming is a very pretty and useful lake and a very large resource of northern Ontario. It is a large resource for southern Ontario as well, because if that lake does not continue to serve the purpose it is serving now, namely as a reservoir for power development, we shall pay very dearly for the loss of it. As a first step the department could make a survey. This is just an example. I know the minister is going to have more examples. I know he is familiar with this matter because the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue has brought it to the attention of the cabinet, of caucus and also of the house.
Let us use New Liskeard as an example. The municipality of New Liskeard has been playing around with one of the tributaries of Lake Timiskaming for a number of years. The erosion of the shore is very great in our area. I am not so very old and I cannot remember too far back, but I am old enough to remember that at the mouth of the Wabi river there was a nice grove of hardwood 90205-6-410
Supply-Public Works
trees which was rather unique in that area because they were oak, and normally oak trees do not grow that far north. Most of these oaks have been killed, the shore has eroded and silt piles up in the mouth of the Wabi river.
More important than that, during heavy rainfalls torrents of water come down the river. The lake is muddy about three quarters of the way across Wabi bay, which is two or three miles wide at this point. This was not true 10 years ago, and certainly not 15 years ago. The lake was relatively clear in the past. Many years ago they did have a very large breakwater in the New Liskeard area, and it protected the shore. Over the years it fell into disrepair. The department said it was not as necessary now as it had been in the past, and this is probably true, but its disrepair resulted in a great increase in the rate of erosion, and this is particularly evident since the breakwater was removed. All I am asking is that we give some consideration to this matter.
It is very hard to go back to mining municipalities and say to them "Let us have a conservation organization." How much better it would be if we did that now rather than wait until we reach the same impasse they reached in the United States in the time of Roosevelt, when he took the initiative to set up the Tennessee valley project. After he set up the project millions and millions of dollars worth of benefit accrued from it, but only because they spent the money to put it in. But really it was a little late. It is not too late yet for us to act. It would not be an expensive proposition to bring about conservation in the Ottawa river watershed and prevent the abuses that are bound to take place if we do not take some action. I hope the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue will rise in his place and say something about this because I believe this problem affects all of us in northern Ontario and northern Quebec. It is a serious problem, Mr. Chairman.
In my opinion we were not smart enough in our part of the country to see that a federal law was passed which would prohibit the driving of logs or having logs floating around in the lake all year round. This is not a little pond that we are talking about; it is a lake 85 miles long and 12 miles wide. It is a large body of water. Of course the federal government is responsible for it. It has passed legislation to establish an upper Ottawa improvement company to be responsible for looking after this particular aspect of lake Timiskaming. I am sure it is possible to call up the people concerned and criticize them for not sweeping the particular area and they will get busy and do

it. I think the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue will agree with me that we should have an authority representative of all the municipalities and communities around the lake. We should be pressing the federal government for this survey and for control dams on the headwaters of that system, which would make it much easier to overcome the silt problem and cut down the amount of clay which is drifting into the lake. The other valuable assets and the natural resource that we have in that area in the form of lake Timiskaming should be protected.
I should like the department to give immediate consideration to the land erosion program as it affects three or four of the municipalities. The municipality of Harris is now a very well developed housing area, but the shore line of the lake is usually in very bad shape. The erosion taking place is not legally the responsibility of the government, because the water level in that area was changed. It was placed so high that you would have to drown the town of New Lis-keard before there was any high water problem. I own a piece of land along the shore there which is four or five acres in extent. I think I would be lucky if I could claim half an acre because the rest of it, owing to the very high water level established at the time they changed the water levels with the erection of the dams in south Timiskaming, would be under water. This appears to me rather unrealistic. Surely the reason for establishing the high water level was not to take away from the federal government its admitted responsibility of preventing and supervising erosion. This has come about because of the inability of the department to decide at the time what the high level should be in relation to the level that would have to be maintained by the dam, and the fact that the government did not want to be put into the position, I am quite sure, of having to expropriate a great deal of land for flooding purposes, if that was necessary, when the level was established in the lake. I may be wrong, but it seems to me that the reference to the high water level was changed in the deeds about the same time that the water level in the lake was raised by the establishment of the permanent dam in south Timiskaming.
I should like to see more municipalities undertake to do their share of the protection of the shore line. New Liskeard has been doing some erosion prevention work. The department of highways is interested in this problem, because there is continuous danger of their losing the highway which until this year has been a part of the trans-Canada system. There is great danger of

the highway falling into the lake. The water comes up very close to the shore line. It is a rocky shore line, and when the water is maintained at a high level the winds and the ice conditions make it very difficult to maintain a sufficient amount of land on the lake side to prevent a threat to the highway. On occasions the road has to be closed off because part of it falls into the water.
It may be true that the water level is too high. It is also true that the municipalities are ignorant of their rights, Mr. Chairman. They have not applied for assistance in the prevention of erosion. In most instances they have done it themselves without any assistance. While this is to be commended, the fact is that they do not necessarily spend their money in the most efficient manner. I think much more could be achieved if they would spend their money in conjunction with financial assistance from the federal government, and they would also be able to avail themselves of the technical advice and assistance that the federal department is quite capable of giving. The department has had a great deal of experience in other parts of the country in connection with erosion and the protection of shore lines, and their assistance would be very valuable. Yet it always seems to require a great deal of dickering to arrive at an arrangement whereby the federal government will participate in these matters. I say the municipalities are partly responsible for this because of their inability to understand just what their responsibility is and what grants are available to them.
I think such projects could be carried out under the winter works program. I know that the town of New Liskeard would be willing to do their erosion work in the late fall and early spring, because the water level is very low at that time and the work could be done more economically then. I would be pleased if the minister would give some indication when he replies as to what the department is going to do with relation to the whole Ottawa river watershed. This question involves considerations of diversion, canalizing the Ottawa, the system of control to be used, the necessary reforestation under a conservation program, what assistance the government will give in setting up a conservation authority like the Thames valley authority and the Tennessee valley conservation authority in the United States; in other words, what assistance the federal government contemplates giving in this whole field in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I should like also to refer to something that does not seem to work too well in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I know that up to May 1960, when regulations to take effect on January 1, 1961 were adopted, loans could be obtained for buildings located in places where there are no sewers.
Not being aware of those new regulations, I recently wrote C.M.H.C. on behalf of Mr. Dupuis. Besides reading the letter I wrote, I will also read the reply I received from the corporation.
Here is what I wrote:
Gentlemen-
Mr. Andre Dupuis, 30 Rouville St., Hull, told me that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation refused to approve a $15,000 loan because his house is to be built along McConnell road, where there is no sewer or water service.
Taking into account the fact that his lot is about 200' x 200', that the septic tank is to be installed at the far end of it, more than 100 feet away from the well, and also taking into account the fact that he has a letter from Dr. Gregoire, Quebec health deputy minister, who after an examination of the plans stated that everything is in accordance with the provincial sanitary regulations, how is it that C.M.H.C. refuses to approve that loan?
I know that Mr. Dupuis has a large family of 10 children and that, because of his difficulties in finding proper housing for them, he is forced to build. Do you not think that those particular circumstances deserve special consideration?
I would be very happy if you would reconsider this case in the light of those facts, and if it is not formally forbidden by the law, try and grant his request.
Here is the answer I received from the Ottawa branch manager. I quote:

His case was considered again and we reached the same decision, that we cannot accept his application since there is no sewer system in a suburban-like area.

Supply-Public Works You will no doubt agree that the area where Mr. Dupuis wants to build has a very good residential development potential for the future, with a sewer system and waterworks planned according to accepted city planning principles.
Our past experience proves that it is difficult to carry out such a program in a suburban area where a number of houses have already been built without any such system.
We are really sorry not to be able to grant his request, but he might perhaps consider another site where a loan could be authorized under our rules.
My point is that at least two houses have been built in that area under a C.M.H.C. loan. In fact, a Mr. Tremblay, if I am not mistaken, and another individual have built houses there after the department of health of the province of Quebec had recognized that their system, according to the blueprints, was acceptable to the department of health.
I realize that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has decided it should protect individuals against themselves, and I realize that preventive measures are called for.
However, in areas where there are no sewage systems and where none will perhaps be installed for years to come, when people comply with provincial government regulations requiring septic tanks to be placed at a distance of at least 30 feet from the well, I fail to see why a change was made to the provision which formerly allowed house building loans to be granted. We must not forget that in our cities, there are large families that cannot find accommodation and must go out and build outside the city, something they might be unable to do if taxes were in relation to the services provided.
Moreover, if loans were granted for this type of housing on the basis of provincial health legislation, this would be a tremendous boon to some areas where there is a great need for accommodation for large families.
I therefore leave the matter with the minister. I hope he will consider it and will agree to amend the regulations so that provincial sanitation regulations will be recognized as reasonable housing standards in areas without sewage systems.
Following a number of members who have spoken before me, I should now like to discuss the matter of retaining walls.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, from time immemorial and up to the years 1954 or 1955, the Department of Public Works has at all times, both under Conservative and Liberal administrations, accepted a measure of responsibility for the construction of such walls.

Supply-Public Works I know such was the practice for at least 30 years, and that it was when Mr. Winters was appointed to the Department of Public Works in Ottawa that the system was changed. I think Mr. Winters was advised by lawyers that he had no right to get into this field and that since then, the department has stuck to the same policy.
I had an opportunity of writing to the minister in that connection not so long ago, that is on August 19, 1960, and in that letter I explained the problem as I saw it.
Dear Sir:
I received your letter of August 13, in reply to mine of July 17, concerning the damage caused by floods in the municipality of South East Buckingham. You mention that the damages resulted from the extraordinary swelling of the waters which occurred last spring. That, I will admit, but the whole question remains debatable. As I stated in the house, Mr. Winters took the liberty of giving his own interpretation to the constitution when he said that all navigable rivers were under the jurisdiction of the federal government. Even if Mr. Winters confused "navigable rivers" and "rivers where there is navigation", I took the matter up with the attorney general of Quebec, who claimed that the responsibility lies with the federal government, since, according to the constitution, the latter is responsible for navigable waters.
I then asked Mr. Winters to take advantage of a federal-provincial conference to clear up this matter, which he never did, and I note that you have accepted this version or interpretation given by Mr. Winters; I am all the more surprised since you are a lawyer and I am convinced that a lawyer would interpret a matter such as this better than an engineer.
To clarify this matter once and for all, it should be submitted to the Minister of Justice and, at the same time, to the attorneys general of the different provinces, so as to establish:
1.	The extent of the federal government's responsibility regarding damages caused by navigable waters;
2.	The complete definition of navigable waters; and
3.	The extent of the principle of overpowering circumstances or, as it is called, an act of God.
Then we should not have to treat those matters in a haphazard way in the future.
Here is the minister's reply, dated October 1:
Re: Flood damage in Buckingham, Que.
Dear Mr. Caron:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter dated August 19, 1960, and I am sorry I have been unable to reply to you sooner.
I have made a thorough study of your comments in connection with this problem and I feel there is a misunderstanding on that point.
Section 91 of the B.N.A. Act gives the parliament of Canada exclusive jurisdiction to legislate in matters pertaining to navigation and shipping. Parliament has exercised that jurisdiction over the years by adopting statutes such as the Canada Shipping Act, the Navigable Waters Protection Act, the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act, etc.

The Canadian government has also carried out its responsibilities in administering that legislation as well as regulations set up under the various acts.
The comments I just made thoroughly prove that the legislative power of the Canadian parliament is restricted to matters which can reasonably be considered as related to navigation and water transport. Those are the limits of parliamentary authority in Canada in this matter.
On this point I do not seem to understand the argument very well. I was told at the start that there is somewhere a misunderstanding with regard to the matter and the government's responsibility is said to be limited to the field of navigation and water transport. Nevertheless, when I submitted that to Mr. Duplessis who, at the time was attorney general of the province of Quebec -Mr. Duplessis was also a lawyer-he said: The waterways are the responsibility of the federal government, and I therefore always insist that the means be found for the two parties to get together in order to know whom to approach. To date there has been no such understanding or discussion, which might have been helpful.
And he says further:
You indicated, in your letter, that waterways are the responsibility of the federal government. The proposition is correct-so the minister told me-as far as you intend it to mean that navigaion and transport on the waterways are constitutionally under the jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament.
The problem you are raising in your letter deals with the responsibility resulting from flood damage to properties on the banks of the Ottawa river, at South East Buckingham, in the spring of 1960. You will recall that the flood was due to heavy rainfall when the river had reached its highest spring level.
The conditions prevailing on the Ottawa river, near South East Buckingham in 1960 can in no way be blamed on or related to navigation or ship-pin.
Therefore the parliament of Canada has no authority under the constitution to pass legislation on such matters.
The problem is essentially "a purely local and private matter in the province" under subsection 16 of section 92 of the British North America Act. The constitution gives jurisdiction in this matter exclusively to the provincial legislature.
I hope this explanation will clearly show the distinction between matters under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada and those under the provincial legislature, and satisfactorily answers your first question.
As to your second question, I might say that the expression "navigable waters" has not been defined by the legislator.
Well, how can we gauge government responsibility with regard to navigable waters, if the expression has never been defined in the law.
Things were left that way on purpose, because each case must be decided on its merits.

This is where my opinion is at variance with the minister's and all those who share this opinion.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I was discussing the second part of the reply, or rather the reply to the second part of my letter dealing with retaining walls. The minister wrote, and I quote:
With reference to your second question, I may say that the phrase "navigable waters" has not been defined in the legislation. This was done on purpose, because it is a matter to be determined in the light of the facts of every particular case. However, the courts have ruled that a river is in fact navigable if, in its natural condition, it can be used for purposes of trade, no matter how the trade is carried on. The standard of navigability of a river must therefore be judged in the light of its natural capacity and its usefulness for trade purposes. The courts have in fact ruled that small rivers of shallow depth in which navigation could only be carried on in small craft were none the less navigable.
Though I am not sure what purpose you have in mind in raising your third question in connection with the present case, I might mention that the phrase "act of God" has been defined in civil law as being "an unforeseen event caused by a major force against which no resistance is possible . Under the law, an act of God is necessarily a very unusual event and is seldom invoked successfully as a means of defence in a damage suit.
The principles applying to the present situation are clear, and I regret being unable to see any advantage in discussing this matter with the attorneys general of the various provinces.
First, I must say that I do not consider the reply as clear as the minister claims it is. I submit that in the minister's letter, there are many contradictions, particularly where he suggests that the responsibility of the federal government mainly concerns navigated waters rather than navigable waters, and quotes as an example the findings of the courts to the effect that shallow rivers and even, if I am not mistaken, a river which perhaps is not normally navigable but on which logs are floated to the mills are considered navigable.
The minister has stated his opinion. I have asked, and I again ask what is the extent of the federal government's responsibility in relation to damage caused by the waters of navigable rivers?
This is a question which has been discussed at great length. I have raised it in Quebec. I have raised it in Ottawa. The opinions

Supply-Public Works
given to me in Ottawa are at variance with the opinions I have received from Quebec. It is claimed in Ottawa, and this is the generally recognized opinion, that navigable waters are a federal responsibility, but that the bed and the river itself are a provincial responsibility in view of the fact that they are the property of the province.
But when I ask both federal and provincial authorities to co-operate in order to clearly define the responsibilities, nobody does anything about it. Neither federal ministers nor provincial ministers take action with a view to finding a method of agreement to define responsibilities.
I do not accept the federal government's version in its entirety; part of it might be correct and based on something sound and reliable. Besides, I do not accept either the provincial government's suggestion that this is a federal responsibility. It seems to me that both governments have a joint responsibility and that they could agree to clearly define it.
The minister says this amazing thing in his letter:
With reference to your second question, I may say that the phrase "navigable waters" has not been defined in the legislation.
Well, if it has not been defined, it is time perhaps we had a sound and complete definition of navigable waters.
We are told that all waters where navigation is possible and on which logs can be floated are navigable waters and that we already have findings to that effect. Well, both governments should meet once and for all in order to discuss this matter and give satisfaction to those who maintain that they have a right to those retaining walls, because if that responsibility were clearly defined and if the present department, like the previous one under Mr. Winters, had accepted to keep on building retaining walls, a great number of projects could be undertaken in many Canadian municipalities, which could alleviate unemployment since local people could carry out such work during the summer.
That is what I am asking the minister. I ask him to kindly see to it that a definite plan be established. This is not my first request on that point. In fact, on December 3, 1957, I asked the minister the following question:
(Text):
Has the minister taken advantage of the federal provincial conference to discuss with the premier of Quebec as to which government is responsible for protection walls along the Ottawa and Gatineau rivers?

(Translation):
I never obtained an answer. And I asked this supplementary question:
(Text):
Is it the intention of the minister to discuss the matter with the Quebec authorities who claim that it is the federal responsibiliy?
(Translation):
I did not get an answer to that question.
I asked another one:
(Text):
Due to the controversy between the Quebec and the federal authorities regarding the responsibility towards the building of protection walls alongside of navigable rivers, even if not or little navigated, would the minister satisfy all the interested parties by submitting the case to the Supreme Court of Canada for clarification?
(Translation):
There again, I got no reply.
Mr. Chairman, I think it is about time that the governments agree on a precise definition as to who is responsible for navigable waters and who is responsible for the prevention of farm land erosion by navigable waters. There is a great deal of farm land in my constituency-the same thing can be said about several other constituencies in Canada-which is being eroded gradually by the water in the spring and in the fall. Farmers who are not rich have lost hundreds of feet of land in a space of 25 years.
The government must attend to that. I am not blaming entirely the federal government and the provincial governments. My criticism is aimed mostly at the ministers who do not want to clear up this matter.
I know that in the committees where there are a lot of lawyers, plays are made on words. But when the question to be cleared up is one of such importance to the people of those areas, it seems to me that they could take the trouble of coming to an agreement to clear up this situation, so that we may know where to apply when damage is caused by some river, whether it be the Ottawa, the Gatineau or any other river.
I know that retaining walls were built at certain places. I am not blaming the ministers who authorized them. However, I feel that that should be the over all policy as it was until 1954 or 1955. That had been the constant practice under all the ministers of public works and all administrations. Municipalities and farmers who had damage caused by erosion always received assistance from the federal government.
And that practice was followed by lawyers. I know that Mr. Fournier, now a judge of the exchequer court, and who was, of course, a lawyer followed that practice. So did his

predecessor, Mr. Cardin, also a lawyer. In short, the ministers of public works who were mostly lawyers, always recognized this as a federal responsibility.
I wonder why there was a change of attitude since that time? If it is only for the sake of economy, I think it ill-advised. Because, such a saving does not help the people. If expenditures were made in different counties to assist the population who suffers damage on account of erosion by water, it would reduce unemployment, since such works would call for local manpower.
That is why I ask the minister once again to take up this matter with the provincial authorities, in order to have a definition of navigable waters, to know who is responsible and to see whether navigable waters must be taken to mean waters on which there is navigation. Let us have a clear definition of these words and we will know if we must direct our requests to the provincial government.
But, pending the clarification of this matter, I submit that we must request the federal Minister of Public Works to revert back to the sound policy that obtained before 1954. That is what I am asking today.
