Mr. Chairman, before coming to the main items which cause me to rise today I should like to support the plea put forward this morning by my colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, for a revision of the government's policy with respect to public buildings in general, and in particular to post office accommodation for small communities.
We raised this matter when the estimates of the Postmaster General were before the committee, and subsequent correspondence which I received from the Postmaster General indicated that we had given him the impression that we were asking for a post office building in every community that has a post office. Of course, that was not so and I should like to take this opportunity to correct that impression.
As my colleague pointed out this morning, we have a special situation in Newfoundland because of the difficulty of integrating the policy of the Newfoundland government prior to our becoming a part of Canada with the policy of the government of Canada. Many small communities which were able to get a public building for post office accommodation from the Newfoundland government prior to confederation, are now smaller than many other communities which have grown since confederation and which are not able to qualify for these buildings under the present

Supply-Public Works
We are not asking for a post office building in every community, but there are many communities where the public cannot be served satisfactorily by the post office being in some part of a person's residence. Particularly in the larger communities which have a population of five or six hundred or a thousand people, we feel the best solution is to have a little post office building. We ask that every case be considered on its merits. There would not be very many; in my own riding there might be five or six communities in that category. So I would urge the minister to consider the details which my colleague has put on record in Hansard and to take another look at this policy respecting postal accommodation in these communities which have grown and expanded since confederation.
I think there is no department of government which touches the lives of so many of my constituents or affects them more closely than the Department of Public Works. I have in my riding about 55,000 people most of whom are dispersed in some 160 small communities stretched along a coast line which, if it were straightened out, would reach for hundreds of miles. It can be realized how important to these people are the services provided by the minister's department. When it is considered that about 80 per cent of these people are fishermen and that all of them are facing the sea-and even those who do not earn their living directly from the sea often use the sea as a highway- we get some idea of the importance of the structures which the Department of Public Works provides. In our smallest communities there is a need either for a little landing place where small boats can dock or for a ramp to help fishermen haul up their boats more easily without damaging them on rocks and boulders.
I know that from a strictly economic point of view many of these structures could not, perhaps, be justified but I raise this question today mainly to point out to the minister that there are factors other than purely economic ones to be considered, and in my opinion these other factors are more important. The usefulness of these structures is not limited to the people who actually live in the settlement. Once a wharf or landing place has been provided it serves the interests of everybody in the area and, from time to time, of people throughout the province or even those who live outside the province. To be able to tie up alongside a wharf in a small boat, instead of having to lie at anchor all night and pass sleepless hours wondering whether the wind might change and your vessel be blown ashore, is a most comforting experience. It is much

Supply-Public Works
better to be able to lie alongside some sound structure and have a good night's sleep without worrying about whether you will have to run for your life or whether you will drift ashore during the night. In our larger communities we need wharves in order that the C.N.R. ships may tie up for the convenience of passengers and for the handling of freight. If such structures do not exist, the work which has to be done is multiplied many times. People have to go out in small boats in all weather to deliver cargo and bring it ashore. Inconvenience is caused especially to old people and to women and children who have to clamber over boulders and climb down rickety stages. All of this could be avoided by the expenditure of comparatively few dollars to build a landing place or small wharf in these communities.
I should like to point out that many of the structures which have been provided so far in many communities have led to a considerable decrease in the cost of living. If a community facing the sea has a harbour and can bring in its coal direct from Sydney or St. John's it can save as much as four or five dollars a ton on that item alone. Multiply the saving by a large number of communities and you will realize the total advantage to the people who live in this region, though the statistics in any one place may not be impressive.
Then there are the breakwaters. These not only provide shelter for the boats which are moored in the harbours but very often they save lives as well. In our winters in Newfoundland we experience very stormy weather and it is not unusual to find waves 14 feet high rolling in on the land. Last winter, in particular, the weather was severe and there were cases reported when walls of water 17 feet high rolled on the beaches. That is the height of a two-storey house, and hon. members can imagine what damage would have been done not only to shipping but to lives and property along the water front if breakwaters had not provided some protection. Last winter in several of the communities in my riding the force of these seas was strong enough to upset several of these breakwaters, but the very fact that they were there saved not only the fishermen's property but their dwellings and, possibly, their lives.
These are all factors which must be taken into consideration apart from strictly economic considerations. I wish to express my appreciation to the minister for the kind and thoughtful attention he has always given to the many cases I have brought to his attention during the last year and for the careful and sympathetic consideration he has always given to them. Since I am speaking mainly of the work of the harbours and engineering

branch I want to pay a special tribute to the chief engineer, the district engineer and the officials of the harbours and rivers engineering service, because it was with them that I had most of my contacts. I have always found them most co-operative in trying to solve the problems and to work out what is best for the fishermen, or for the community concerned.
I note that the vote for harbours and engineering services in Newfoundland is up this year by about $316,000. I realize that a large part of this amount is earmarked to take care of the contracts that have been let with respect to St. John's harbour. I do hope that this large project will soon reach completion and that the minister will then be able to give more consideration to these smaller works which I have brought to his attention.
I mentioned a while ago, Mr. Chairman, that I have 160 settlements in my riding. I think I could find something that would be useful and needed in each one of them, but I assure the minister I am not going to make a list of them. There is already on record in the department a list of recommendations that will take care of his votes in this regard for perhaps several years to come, but I do want to mention one particular place, perhaps two. I am not going to go into detail about it because I have already given the minister complete details in a volume of correspondence. The place I refer to is Seal Cove in Connaigre bay. I brought up this matter in his predecessor's day. It has been deferred from one year to another. I merely mention it now to point out to the minister that the situation is getting more and more desperate the longer it is deferred. This is a large, important and growing community. The provincial government has lived up to its part of the bargain in this instance. They put the road to the new site. I do hope that the minister will see fit to include in his estimates next year an item to provide a sort of combination breakwater-wharf which is necessary to provide a harbour for those people and also to permit them to earn a livelihood because if this is not done they will have no means of earning a living at all.
I should like to bring one other place to the attention of the minister, namely the town of Marystown. The town of Marystown has a public wharf which is pretty much in the same condition today that it was 10 years ago when Newfoundland became a part of Canada. It has been repaired and strengthened, but it is not at all in keeping with the kind of facility the department has provided for other communities of similar size and importance. This picture is not now adequate to the needs of Marystown. Again this is a

structure that has been deferred from year to year. I do hope the minister will make a special note of this along with Seal Cove. I should be very happy if he can have these two items in his estimates next year.
One other point I should like to mention to the minister has to do with policy or perhaps I should say priority. I know it makes a very good argument to say that if a community has a road, then its need for a wharf is thereby lessened. Well, that argument is not as sound as it appears because the road that it has is usually very poor; it is not a paved road; it is just a small narrow dirt road, usually very dangerous and usable only for a very short part of the year. To truck freight over that kind of road is very costly.
Despite the fact that communities seven or eight miles away, may be linked up with other settlements by road, I would ask the minister to keep in mind that during the wintertime the road will be blocked and nothing will be able to get over it. There is still need for an outlet by the sea, and that can only be had by providing the proper facilities.
I have one particular case in mind that I wish to bring to the minister's attention in this regard, namely Harbour Mille in Fortune bay. I understand it is not the fault of the department that this structure has been delayed so long. There again the situation is getting more and more acute. The population and the need are growing. Therefore I ask the minister to reconsider this project and see what can be done in his estimates next year.
During the past two years there has been a great deal of rumour and press reports in my riding about the development of a transshipment harbour at Mortier bay. I understand an interdepartmental committee has been considering this project for many years. There is so much rumour that I think it would be advisable to have some official pronouncement about this project in so far as it concerns the minister's department. If the minister can reveal anything of any plans in the process of being worked out for this project I would be very grateful to him if he would tell us about it when he replies.
Then there is need for clarification of policy with respect to erosion. As has been pointed out by a good many hon. members, at the present time it is difficult to define where federal responsibility ends and provincial responsibility begins. If the federal department accepts responsibility for erosion caused by lakes and rivers, it would seem to me logical that that policy should apply also to harbours and to the approaches to harbours. I personally would like to see a clear-cut definition of policy with respect to protection works to take care of erosion of the sea shore.
Supply-Public Works
There are two other matters that I wish to mention before I take my seat. I notice that the vote for repairs and upkeep, vote 358, has been reduced by $100,000. This happens to be the year when we have the most need of repairs, following the very severe winter that we have just gone through, with all the storm damage that I mentioned a few minutes ago. I do hope that this reduction in the vote will not delay the necessary repairs to put those structures back into shape before another winter comes.
I am glad to see that vote 360 for dredging, construction or acquisition of plant and equipment, has been increased by $366,000. That is a relatively small increase. I do not think the minister will be able to secure very much new equipment with that much money. As I have pointed out on previous occasions, dredging is one of our most urgent needs in Newfoundland. Although we have modern equipment, we do not have any heavy suction dredging equipment. We have been trying for two years to pry loose the dredge of that type operating in Nova Scotia but it seems to be stuck there, and in the meantime our needs are becoming more and more acute. There is certainly a need for more heavy suction dredging equipment than we have and there is also a need for more shallow dredging equipment.
I hope the minister will look at this need, particularly with regard to Newfoundland, because the amount of equipment we have there now has not been able to look after the needs that were inherited ten years ago when Newfoundland became part of Canada and very soon some of these situations will have to be looked at again. If we are going to keep abreast of the problem and maintain our harbours in proper shape, we must have more dredging equipment than we have at the present time.
I am a little disappointed that vote 371 for miscellaneous works is slightly less than last year. It is now $2,450,000 compared with $2,500,000 last year. This is a reduction of $50,000 but certainly the trend is in the wrong direction. If there is one vote that needs to be increased more than any others, it is that for miscellaneous works not otherwise provided for. Most of the structures in small communities in my riding of the type to which I referred earlier have to be financed from this vote. Many of these communities have been waiting for six or seven years now for something to be done. Because the amounts are too small to be listed separately in the blue book, this is one vote that should be doubled instead of decreased.
When one considers that the $2,450,000 has to be distributed all across Canada from the

Supply-Public Works
Atlantic to the Pacific, it is certainly not a very large sum. When one considers further that projects costing up to $25,000 can now be financed out of this vote, it becomes apparent that no provision has been made for the extra drain on this fund. To reduce the total amount only makes the drain all the heavier and will certainly result in deferring still longer many small projects costing $3,000, $4,000 or $5,000 for which we have already been waiting for several years.
I am not going to burden the minister with further details. I have tried to speak in general terms, but I hope the minister will heed what I have just said about the need for a further increase in the dredging vote and particularly in the vote for miscellaneous works. Finally, I thank the minister and his officials again for what they have done in the past and I hope they will be able to do even more in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I am grateful for the opportunity to speak briefly on the general item of these estimates. I represent Leeds, a riding in the very heart of what has been characterized as the golden triangle of eastern Ontario. Various tourist publications describe the area as being directly north of New York state, a land of hundreds of clear lakes, sparkling trout streams, thousands of picturesque islands, lofty evergreens, rugged mountains and so on. It is a lot more than that, Mr. Chairman, but may I say that under earlier administrations certain great projects flowed from the co-operation of Mr. King and Mr. Roosevelt first of all with respect to the Thousand Islands bridge at Ivy Lea. In respect of that bridge I think that a tribute should be paid to a man who worked indefatigably for it for many years long before it became a reality. I refer to George Fulford. He travelled up and down eastern Canada and particularly upstate New York. The Ivy Lea bridge is just over 300 miles from New York city, the most populous and wealthy part of the United States of America. It is right in the centre of that golden triangle bounded on the east by the charming village of Bainsville, on the north by Hawkesbury, the Ottawa river and Deep river and on the south by that ancient, great and historic city of Kingston.
The Thousand Islands bridge at Ivy Lea, in which Mr. Fulford had so much interest in years past, has actually transformed the face of eastern Ontario. Unquestionably my riding, all of which is within 40 miles of the bridge, is vitally interested in tourism. Extending to the west we have historic sites as far as Kingston. Extending to the east we have Glengarry park, Upper Canada village and so many of the great areas along the river

including the parks of the parks commission which are now attracting thousands of United States tourists to this country.
We now see indications that the Canadian dollar appears to be slipping and no doubt this will lead to greater tourism, particularly if the minister can impress upon his colleagues the urgency and importance at least to our part of Canada of soft-pedalling anti-Americanism. Those of us who live in this part of Canada feel that we are very closely related to upstate New York and, indeed, to all of the United States. We feel that our wealth is partly dependent upon a happy and close relationship with the United States and we believe that at times definite harm has been done to our area by comments that have been made and by policies that have done our area no particular good.
It happens that the Leeds area, which has such attractive places as Gananoque, Seeleys Bay and Westport on the west, Charleston and the Rideau lakes system, is very popular with United States tourists and a most happy relationship exists between our people and them. We hope that this relationship will continue to exist.
We were pleased when the minister spoke on May 25 last of a contract having been let for a public wharf at Westport. Westport is only a tiny place but it is immensely important. It is located on a beautiful body of water which is connected with other bodies of water and it is really important so far as the tourist business is concerned.
The minister also spoke of Seeleys Bay, which was the home of my very fine predecessor, Mr. Hayden Stanton. Seeleys Bay is also important from the tourist standpoint. On May 24 the minister also referred to contracts that have already been let at Gananoque and other work to be performed. I would impress upon the minister that anything that is done in this area in the way of public works, however small it may be, will add to the general economy, welfare and benefit of this part of Canada. We do not expect from the minister, perhaps, great projects of the type of the deep sea waterway or such things as the Thousand Islands bridge. These works have already been completed and the whole area has been elevated and enriched by the co-operation, for example, that existed between Mr. St. Laurent and, in the first instance, Mr. Truman. This has transformed this part of Canada. Still, the natural beauties are there. They are very much appreciated and we can go forward with new heart.
I urge the minister kindly consider, from the standpoint of unemployment, any of these projects in that part of the riding which is bounded on the north by Smiths Falls, on the

east by Brockville, on the south by Ganano-que, and on the west by Westwood, because they are very urgently needed at this particular time.

Has the minister considered the advisability of constructing better looking post offices? Many complaints have been received from all parts of Canada about the new post office buildings, especially in so far as the small post offices are concerned. These buildings are erected by the federal government, and if they do not look well in their surroundings they give the appearance that the federal government is the poor member of the family.
I know the minister agrees that, since there are so many complaints, there should be some improvement.
I know that in the province of Quebec a committee has been formed to study the decoration of public buildings, and this commute is composed of architects and painters.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I regret the situation in Rouyn. They needed more space and it was a question of adding to the present post office or getting a new site altogether. I understand the original building was constructed in 1956 or so. It was not considered practical to scrap it and so an addition was planned on the same architectural design as the building constructed in 1954 or 1956. One consequence- and I think it is regrettable-is that it comes up very close to the street line. It is not set back. However, now that the exterior has been cleaned up around there it is looking much better. I agree that, if we could have done so, it would have been better to get rid of the old building. However, these things must be looked at from an economic standpoint. I agree that if we could have got rid of the old post office there and could have built a brand new one, it would have looked much better because we could have given it more space. However, we had to add to it under the circumstances.

In view of the fact that the minister has mentioned the post office in Rouyn which is in my constituency, I think he would like me to correct an assertion just made by him to the effect that the building was constructed in 1954. It was constructed long before 1954. It was built in the 40's or in the 30's. I agree that the government did the right thing by putting on an addition to this building. However, this is only a one-storey addition and it does not look too good.

speechtext: Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, I raised three or four problems in relation to the public buildings in Ottawa. Then there is the problem that is uppermost in the minds of many people who are interested in agricultural development and experimental work. It is in connection with the difference of opinion that appears to exist as to whether the experimental farm should be considered to be a land assembly scheme on which any department can put government buildings if they cannot find a site somewhere else. The other side of the coin, as it were, represents the opinion that no buildings should be constructed on the experimental farm except those that are closely allied and connected with the continuation and the furthering of agricultural experimental work.
Which coin?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I wish to admit to the hon. member that I am no authority on town planning. However, the former government brought in from France probably the greatest town planner in the world-I refer to Mr. Greber-and he submitted a plan to the predecessor of the national capital commission for a more beautiful and greater Ottawa. After many adjustments his plan was approved by the national capital commission, the government of Canada and the city of Ottawa. It is a decentralized plan, but in being a decentralized plan it follows the tendencies of Madrid, Paris, London and latterly Washington. I should like to be able to engage with my hon. friend in a learned talk on this subject. However, in matters of this kind, I always rely on experts. However, I would think that his views might be brought up for consideration in committee at some time or other. There is certainly an argument for what he has said as certain people object to decentralization.

While these alterations and improvements are being made in the west block and other buildings, would it be possible to have a kind of recreational centre to which members of parliament could go and take some exercise? As the minister himself has noticed, and other people have noticed this, we are far from healthy and one only has to look around to see the big bellies which are caused by lack of exercise.
In past years members of parliament, their wives, staff, messengers and newspaper men used to be able to bowl-and paid plenty of money for it-outside the parliament buildings. I am sure this could be done by charging a fee less than we used to pay outside.
I am sure it would be a good thing for the members of parliament and the staff to have this kind of recreational centre. As the hon. member for Kootenay West has just said, there might be less sissies around and more people would be physically fit for work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If there is to be such a recreational centre, would the minister make sure it includes a punching bag?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I could have used one the last couple of days. I have been sitting here silently for two days. In answer to my hon. friend from St. Denis may I say that there is to be an exercise room on the top floor of the west block, and also showers in connection with it. It will not be a large room. I understand that many members of the opposition and the Leader of the Opposition himself are very much concerned about the leisure of hon. members, but since this question has been raised I should like to bring one matter to the attention of the minister.
I should like to know whether there are provisions for parlours in the west block for people who might be visiting their members of parliament. I can understand that this might not be a question which interests hon. members from far away, but hon. members whose constituencies are not far from Ottawa often have to receive visitors, and it is very difficult for them to find a convenient place in which they can wait. These people have to wait to see their member of parliament in order to discuss some matter with him.
At the moment we have to share an office with another member of parliament, and when we have visitors it disturbs our partner.
I understand that when hon. members' offices are transferred to the west block we will not have to share offices and each member of parliament will have his own. However, we still will not have a waiting room for visitors, I understand. It might be convenient to put such a waiting room on each floor at least. We could have one parlour on each floor, with a telephone, for accommodating visitors who have a right to come and see their member of parliament in Ottawa.
While I am on my feet-and I will try not to rise again-I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that every time hon. members whose constituencies are not far from Ottawa come to Ottawa during the recess, they are very much concerned because they cannot telephone unless the Department of Public Works is notified that the hon. member intends to stay in his office for quite a while. If that is the case, the department sees to it that we have a telephone. If the member of parliament comes

to Ottawa for only one day, I understand he does not have any telephone facilities. I also understand that if an hon. member comes from the Union station to the House of Commons at 10.30 in the morning he has to run in order to get a secretary, and the secretaries leave at 4.00 o'clock during the recess. By the time the member reaches the minister or an official of the Department of Public Works, for instance-the minister has his offices way on the other side of the city- it is difficult for the minister to do anything.
It is sometimes important that members of parliament should phone ministers or departments from the House of Commons, and if they come to Ottawa for only one day they have a very difficult time finding a telephone in order to reach the minister or the officials of his department.
Would it be possible to establish at least pay phones in some parts of the building, either in the main building or the west block, for use during the recess? The best thing to do would be to have telephones at the convenience of hon. members, of course; but if the government is too poor to do that, at least let it put pay phones in different sections of the building and in the waiting rooms. They could be put in the corridors or the hallways of the west block and on the main floor of the centre block.
In reply to my hon. friend I shall be glad to take up that matter with the Speaker because this is something which is within his purview.

May I ask whether funds have been provided both for the acquisition of such property and for the construction of this $500,000 building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I should say to the hon. member that the planning vote is for the purpose of doing just what we are doing at the present time. It is not allocated to any particular project.
May I ask the minister when he expects the plans to be completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Some time during the winter. You mean the Brockville federal building?
Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I ask the minister what land the federal government holds in the town of Haileybury and if this is sufficient land upon which to build a post office? I

Supply-Public Works also should like to know if it is contemplated building a post office on that land or whether the department intends to acquire a new site. I understand that the lease of the present building expires in October, and so this question has to be decided in a few months. I believe the federal government does own the armoury site and maybe one or two lots close to it, but I am curious to know whether this is sufficient to allow for the construction of a government building.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I wish to thank the hon. member for Timiskaming. We shall be glad to have the help of any advice he has to give us in this connection. It is not too late to consider that advice, because the whole plan is now under study-whether it is possible to expand or whether we shall have to put up an entirely new building. The hon. member's assistance would be welcomed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wonder if the minister can
tell me when it is anticipated that the federal building in Elliot Lake will be completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It is 97 per cent complete and when it is completed and we go up there I intend to ask the Leader of the Opposition to come along for the opening ceremony.

speechtext: I think that is a good idea. The minister might need a little protection up there.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We anticipate that construction will commence early next summer if the Kingston firm has completed its plans and if everything works out as we anticipate.

On May 24 the minister was good enough to indicate there would be a new post office at Portland costing $25,000. Has property been acquired for the post office at Portland? When will tenders for this building be called?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: This is a winter works program. We will seek the information from our officials and I shall let the hon. member know as soon as it is received.

I asked a question on behalf of the hon. member for Niagara Falls. I said she was attending a committee. An hon. member to my left, I think it was the member for Medicine Hat, suggested that that was not right. She is in the railway committee room at the present time. speechtext: By the middle or end of July this year.
Will tenders be called immediately thereafter?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission

speechtext:

speechtext: It will be a winter works program, starting this fall in October.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
340.	British Columbia, $2,680,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I do not play that game any more.

speechtext: The Rossland extension or alternation is now under study and when the study is completed the alterations will be proceeded with. portion of the federal government's housing programs in these two locations?

speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question about an item in this vote that deals with the Canada House building in London, England, on Grosvenor square. What is the total expenditure that has been made on the property, on the building itself and on the remodelling that was required?

speechtext: Is there any further expenditure required or is the building now complete, occupied and used?

Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: So that within a short time, when these difficulties to which the minister has referred are cleared up, we can anticipate that all Canadian government offices, except those in the old Canada House, will be in this building and there will be no outside leases in London at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission

speechtext: I am afraid I cannot enlighten the hon. member. It is a matter for external affairs.
Is there an office of the Department of Public Works in Europe since we are looking after all these buildings, and what kind of a staff is there?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Can the minister inform the committee what the exact responsibilities of the Department of Public Works are in connection with Canadian buildings abroad, diplomatic and trade commissioner buildings and that sort of thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
We give the Department of External Affairs any technical assistance they may require. Having learned from them what they wish, we assist them with the plans. When a decision has been reached in conjunction with the Department of External Affairs,

we then proceed to erect the building or arrange the lease or do whatever else is required.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the correspondence we receive continually from the graphic arts association of Montreal about the printing bureau, I should like to ask the minister some questions. I understand that everything in connection with the bureau is paid for by this department, the upkeep, maintenance, lighting, heating and so on. What charge is made to the printing bureau for all these services?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No charge.

No charge whatever. It is all at government expense. The reason I ask the question is that there seems to be quite a controversy between the printers in private industry and the government printing bureau. The bureau claims it can do work much more cheaply than private industry. If they are provided with their building free of charge and are also provided with heating, lighting and everything else free of charge, their costs must be very much lower than those of private printers who have to erect their own buildings, pay taxes and all the other charges.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I do not think I can make any comment. I have completely forgotten about the printing bureau. I think it was three years ago since I had anything to do with it.

In order that there might be a basis for a fairer comparison between the costs of private industry and those of the government-owned plant, would it not be possible for the minister in some way to arrive at a charge that could be made for these services so that there would be some method of arriving at the costs of the government plant? They do not seem to have any basis whatever now. If there is no charge made to them for their plant, lighting, heating or the machinery they buy, it seems unjust for the government plant to say that they can manufacture more cheaply than private industry because the bureau has no basic figures in order to arrive at their costs. If you have a plant worth $5 million and do not have to pay rent or interest or carry anything on your books, it seems obvious that you cannot have any basic figures to indicate that you can manufacture more cheaply. The government will never know whether or not it is losing money in this plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for his comments. This is matter for the Secretary of State, and I understand it is presently under study not only by the Auditor General but also by the public accounts committee.

speechtext: We have had a discussion recently relating to recreational facilities for the members of the House of Commons. speechtext: Because of the manner in which the hon. member has pressed this matter, and the justness of his claim, it is not only being looked into but I expect something will be done about it.

Last year the minister said he would give consideration to the cost of restoring this walk between the parliament buildings and the Ottawa river. Has any consideration been given to the matter, and has there been an estimate of the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I know that the hon. member has a particular interest in this walk. I accept his word that it is purely a platonic interest. I know he is a great admirer of nature. I regret that I must deny the hon. member anything, but I am afraid I must be governed by the advice I get from these two departments.

I thank the minister for his explanation. I can understand, to some extent, the reasons for this stand. However, I was the spokesman for a great many members of his own party who did not have the courage to get up and speak about it.

My Colleague, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska being absent,

Supply-Public Works
has asked me to ask the minister whether or not a decision has been taken concerning repairs to the clock in the public building at Arthabaska. The minister will recall that Arthabaska is a historical place in the province of Quebec because Sir Wilfrid Laurier stayed there for many years.
The minister wrote my colleague on May 18 of this year telling him that if the repairs could be made, they would be made. I know that in the past this question of repairing clocks in public buildings has been a headache for the department because there have been so many complaints from people. However, since this is a historical place, the people would like to keep that old building and the clock, and I wonder if special attention could be given to these minor repairs?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Yes, I will have that looked into at once.

speechtext:

I noticed lately that a competition was advertised by the civil service commission for a purchasing agent at Quebec city. I am asking the minister if any changes have been made in the purchasing department. If I remember correctly, there was a regional staff set up by the Department of Public Works for supplying what was needed for public buildings. I am asking whether any change has been made in this practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: There has been no change. There was a vacancy to be filled.

Are the materials needed for public buildings supplied by Ottawa or by the regional office in Montreal? I do not want to translate this advertisement, Mr. Chairman, because it might be too long, but it sets out in French the functions of the purchasing agent as follows:
(Translation):
To carry out instructions given by the chief of purchasing and stores for the proper operation of the stores-
So, if I understand correctly, in this case-
(Text):
This purchasing agent will be required to buy some materials, and that is why I was wondering if a change had been made and a regional office had been established in Quebec city. I have no objection. I think it would be a good place to establish a purchasing office because it would be centralized. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: While we are looking up the answer to the last question, may I answer the hon. member's question about engineers and architects who resigned in Toronto and Montreal. Mr. A. Gagnon, a district engineer, resigned on May 2, 1961, to join as deputy minister for the Montreal area the provincial service of Quebec; Mr. P. R. Martineau, district architect at Montreal, also resigned on May 2, 1961 to join in a high post the provincial service at Quebec. In Toronto, Mr. K. A. Rowswick, engineer grade 3, resigned on March 31, 1961 to accept a position with a private firm.

May I revert for just a moment to item 344. I am not one of those Conservative members who appointed the hon. member for Kootenay West to act as his spokesman. I should like to speak for myself. I think the reasons given by the police and the national capital commission are utterly inadequate.
I am very pleased to have a supporter in this one man crusade, which has now become a two man crusade.

I was wondering if those officials who resigned from the service left the service because they could not get an increase in salary. These officials had a good deal of experience. The minister and probably the deputy minister also must realize that it is very difficult-and I am speaking of Quebec particularly-to get architects and engineers of experience. I know it is not the fault of the minister because he cannot prevent that situation. However, if it is a question of salaries I think it should be looked into. I think some increase should be given to these men who have rendered service for many years. The time will come when the department-and this statement applies not only to the Department of Public Works but to other departments which are concerned with the construction business- will have great difficulty in getting architects and engineers of good standing and good experience. I know that because I was with the engineers and the architects of the department for four years.
I think we are extremely fortunate to get such good and experienced men having regard to the very small salaries they are getting. When we consider the fact that we are spending nearly $100 million in building and that on harbours and rivers we are spending about $35 million or possibly more, I think the question should be looked into and that an effort should be made to see that they get salaries which are comparable to those being paid in private industry. Some people might think that this is an unnecessary expenditure, but I do not think so. The minister

realizes that when we have good and experienced engineers and architects we are saving to the country every year thousands and thousands of dollars. I therefore think the minister would not be criticized if he looked into the question and, if there is a chance to do so, gave consideration to the salaries of those employees who have experience and whom I think we should keep at the service of Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers engineering services- Construction, acquisition, major repairs and improvements of, and plans and sites for, harbour and river works listed in the details of the estimates, including expenditures on works on other than federal property, provided that treasury board may increase or decrease the amount within the vote to be expended on individual listed projects-
347. Newfoundland, $6,593,500.

I should like to make one or two comments with regard to the amount of money that is spent under this heading in Newfoundland. I think that most of us recognize that the work going on in St. John's is a special job; and as a special project I do not see any reason why the amount of money being spent on this project in one area should be taken from the rest of the province. I think that the money being spent on this project at St. John's is going to be well worth the effort; but because it is a special project, I think that a special grant should have been made for it and that the money to be spent there should not have been taken from projects in other parts of the island.
If we look back over the amounts of money spent in various years under this item in Newfoundland, we find that the amount has been consistently decreasing since 1958-59. I should like to support that statement by some figures which I have here. Expenditures on harbours and rivers for the year 1955-56 amounted to $3,173,601. For 1956-57 the amount was $2,741,601. For the year 1957-58, the amount spent under this item was $3,015,100. For the year 1958-59-and I think this is the first year in which there was in the estimates an item for improvements to the St. John's harbour-the total amount under this heading was $4,606,500, with $1 million for harbour improvements at St. John's leaving for the remainder of the province $3,606,500. For the year 1959-60, the amount under this vote was $4,237,200. The allocation for St. John's harbour was $1,250,000, leaving the total of $2,987,200 for other projects in the province. Last year the total amount under this item was $6,277,501, with harbour improvements in St. John's at $4,500,000, leaving $1,777,501 for the remainder of the province.
Supply-Public Works
Last year the amount spent outside the city of St. John's on harbours and rivers was only slightly more than one-half the amount spent in the same area in 1958-59. 1 am sorry; I should say it was a little more than one half the amount spent in the year 1955-56 and only a little less than one half of the amount spent in the year 1958-59, or I should point out that the total amount of money spent under this heading last year was divided in this manner: 72 per cent for harbour improvements in St. John's and 28 per cent for the whole remainder of the province. This year the estimate gives a total of $6,593,500 and for the St. John's project $4,850,000 leaving $1,743,500 for other projects within the province. For this year it means that the total amounts spent on the St. John's project will be 74 per cent of the total expenditure for the province, with the remaining projects in the province receiving only 26 per cent. Again, the amount for this year is slightly less than half of what was spent in the year 1955-56 and a little less than half of what was spent in 1958-59. I think that anyone who wants to examine these figures carefully will note that since 1958-59 the amount spent under this item outside the city of St. John's has been decreasing consistently.
I hasten to point out to the minister that I am not objecting to the amount of money being spent in St. John's. My contention is that since this is a special item there should be a special vote and that it should not be carried out at the expense of the rest of the province. Around the island of Newfoundland and Labrador, of course, there are many projects in need of being undertaken. It appears to me that some of these projects are being delayed because of the large amount of money being spent on the St. John's project. At this time I am not going to go into any long description of specific points in my riding that need attention. However, I wish to take two particular areas as examples. I refer first to the strait of Belle Isle in the northern part of Newfoundland. I have written to the minister on a number of occasions not only about the area known as the strait of Belle Isle but also for every specific place in that area. Here these people are all fisher folk. I cannot see how they can manage to carry on their work unless the facilities which they cannot be expected to provide for themselves are provided for them. They are living in an area where rough seas are very common and it is impossible for these men to protect their boats unless they are hauled up in the evening and launched in the morning.
The hon. gentleman, being a small boat owner, will know exactly what I mean. I

Supply-Public Works
recognize that in the area in which he operates his boat the waters may be a little bit calmer than they are in the strait of Belle Isle, but I am sure he has some conception of what I am talking about. I have not had the opportunity of seeing the ability with which the hon. gentleman manoeuvers his boat, or should I call it prowess in this case, but I am sure he does it well enough to be able to understand the difficulty of a man in the northern part of Newfoundland who has to handle a big boat in stormy weather.
I also recognize, and I think the minister recognizes this too, that this is not an area where marine works can be built cheaply. In some places where marine works are urgently required it may be true that they will cost a little more than in the average place in Newfoundland. However, I cannot accept that as an argument against having these projects carried out.
In this section of Newfoundland we have one of the few places on the eastern seaboard of Canada where people make their living almost entirely from the fishery. Again I appeal to the minister to give consideration to the representations that have been made on behalf of these people who live and work in the straits of Belle Isle. While it may be true that some of the projects recommended would cost a considerable amount of money, I think the amount of money which might be spent on these projects is small when compared to the return the fishermen will get.
One of our problems in the fishing industry of Newfoundland is that we are not able to get our men working early enough in the year and we are not able to get them working late enough in the fall because they have no protection for their boats. I hope that in an effort to keep these men in their own occupation-one which means that no other type of employment will have to be found for them-this money will be spent. It will be money well spent, and again I describe it by saying that it would be well spent in providing for them those marine works which they could not be expected to provide for themselves.
Again I want to bring to the attention of the minister, as I have on a number of other occasions, the situation in the peninsula of Port au Port. Port au Port is a peninsula that juts out into the sea on the west coast of Newfoundland. It has over 25 small and large communities and exists on the outskirts of the large United States base at Harmon field. Over the last 20 years people from the Port au Port peninsula have been able to earn a living by doing construction work on this United States leased base. Obviously this construction work cannot continue, and as

construction begins to taper off some other alternative employment must be found for these people.
It seems to me that if alternative employment is to be found, it must be found by using the resources that exist in the area. In this particular area there is an ample supply of various types of fish, from the catching of which men could make a living. Here again the shore line is rather rugged. The cost of marine works will be higher than the average, but again I believe that if employment is to be found for these men, to a large extent it will have to be found in the fishing industry. However, these men will certainly be unable to carry out their work as fishermen unless they have the marine works that will provide all the protection and all the convenience they require.
I have had a good deal of conversation and correspondence with the minister concerning what he very affectionately refers to as the Irish town of Piccadilly. Another admirable site for marine construction would be Port au Port. I can also think of Ship Cove, Boswarlos and Mainland. These are places where there are large numbers of fishermen and yet there is no marine protection at all for their fishing boats.
I hope the minister will give some consideration to the needs of the people who live in the strait of Belle Isle and those people who live on the Port au Port peninsula. Last year and the year before I made some recommendations to the minister regarding a settlement on the St. Barbe coast known as Parson's Pond. Some dredging is needed at Parson's Pond. The minister has advised me that a certain amount of dredging will be done there this year.
I am very pleased to hear that and perhaps the minister will not mind if I just say this to him, knowing the situation as I do-and I know it from firsthand experience-and knowing, too, something about the sea.
I do not think that the work the minister intends having done this year will be sufficient to solve the actual problem. It may be that the minister has in mind doing this work and seeing what happens, and then perhaps completing the job another year. If this is all the department intends doing at Parson's Pond I would very respectfully suggest to the minister that a second look should be taken in regard to this matter.

speechtext: We will do that.

I think the dredging that is going to be done will be of some advantage, but whether or not that advantage will last very long is a matter which will have to be decided. I will be very pleased if the minister

goes ahead with what he has decided to do this year, but I think another look should be given to this problem of Parson's Pond.
Mr. Chairman, I know that all around the coast of Newfoundland there are various projects that need attention. I hope that when the minister makes his estimates next year the amount of money he will spend on projects outside the city of St. John's will be restored to the former amount.

I trust tempers will be restrained for a few minutes, as I should like to speak about a few projects on the Magdalen islands. As you well know, Mr. Chairman, our people are humble, but they still have the pioneer spirit. They wish to earn their own living without having to call too often on the government for means of subsistence.
On the Magdalen islands there are, as hon. members know, a number of fishing harbours. The present government has done a great deal of work which has enabled our fishermen to pursue their calling more efficiently. However, there are further harbours, unloading docks and facilities needed to enable them to take advantage of every day of the month and of every month of the year. In some instances we find 50 fishermen fishing out of one harbour while the following month there may be 100 fishermen fishing out of there. In these circumstances the facilities are not sufficient to accommodate them all. I trust the department will take into consideration the fact that this situation does exist and that further developments might well be undertaken.
I can assure the minister and his officials that what has been done is deeply appreciated by those people. I should like to mention a few places to which I believe consideration needs to be given, among them, Oyster Basin where the development of a harbour and not the establishment of a fish processing plant is desired. I understand the department requests that we should have an assurance from the department of fisheries of the province of Quebec that the province will consider moving its fish processing establishment to this area before the government will consider a further development there. However, (he problem there is not to give facilities for fish processing but to be able to harbour the boats which fish out of the area.
I was down in the riding recently and at Old Harry I saw fishermen having to pull their fishing boats over a sand bank between 50 yards and a 100 yards wide before they could get out into deep water. I assure the minister this is not what we expect our fishermen to have to do today. Therefore I suggest that at Old Harry the construction

of a slipway should be immediately undertaken. At Gros lie where the fishermen go in the fall of the year and where there are not sufficient fishing facilities, I would ask for an extension to the present wharf and breakwater. At Havre Maison, or Harbour House, where there are now three different harbour facilities I would recommend that one main harbour be built for the whole island. This would result in a lessening of the expense which the department now has to incur due to sand. Bryan island is the most prolific fishing area of the Magdalen islands although there are no inhabitants there. Since it is situated approximately 15 miles from the main island, many of our fishermen go there on Mondays and return on Friday nights. They are requesting an unloading facility there. Although the land which is owned by one of the co-operatives consists of a few acres I think there is sufficient land on this 600-acre island to be able to build the unloading facility and to give the residents of the Magdalen islands a most prolific area where they can go and earn a living.
At Etang du Nord the problem is very well known. Last year reconstruction of the breakwater was cancelled owing to the fact that the petitioners could not agree on the plan submitted. I trust that the department will undertake another plan immediately and thus be in a position to start this development as soon as possible.
