I have a few observations to make on this item. Probably they could more appropriately have been made on item 1 of the estimates. However, I thought it would be more co-operative to make them at this time. Generally, and before getting to specifics, I should like through the minister to congratulate Mr. Walkey, the chief engineer of harbours and rivers for the British Columbia and Yukon area, on a magnificent job of work done over the past several years. I should like to add to that the very profound thanks of thousands of people in the lower mainland for the splendid work he has done in connection with the planning committee of the port of Vancouver.
I would say, Mr. Chairman, that the discussion this afternoon has been most interesting. I will also say to the minister it has been somewhat disturbing for we have listened for some time during the discussion of these estimates, particularly those on harbours and engineering, to some of our fellow colleagues from the province of Newfoundland sitting in the opposition. It does seem to me there is internal disagreement as to where the vast sum of money allotted to the province should go, whether it should go to the main harbour and port of St. Johns, or whether it should be more generally distributed.
I would say, against this background, and I do hope the minister will pay attention to this, it is indeed disturbing, while we are talking about the distribution of funds, to see amounts such as that allotted to Newfoundland. I say this not for the sake of being parochial in any way whatsoever. It is disturbing when we look at the vast coast lines of the province of British Columbia, including an island certainly in economic importance, in area, and in boat requirements greater than the province of Prince Edward Island, and see a sum of a little over $2
6518	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works
million to supply the public works requirements, the boat shelters, the rock-filled breakwaters that are so urgently needed in so many areas of British Columbia.
I say quite frankly, Mr. Chairman, that I look with some alarm at the general breakdown of these items under harbours and engineering services, and I would ask the minister to take a very careful look at this matter in future years and try to establish a balanced program based on the economic needs of various areas of Canada and making provision for the safety of the thousands of craft that are plying the waters off our shores.
I wish to thank the minister for certain splendid undertakings such as that going forward at Okeover arm and the Westview small boat harbour. I wish to discuss these briefly. They are of a somewhat different concept in the provision of shelter on the west coast. They are rock-filled shelters where small craft can go for a short period or for a longer moorage. I would very much wish the minister to take cognizance of the fact that, though these works have been done and are appreciated, much of the thanks should go to the people living along that coast. I consider, and I am sure the minister will agree, that they have co-operated in a most wholehearted way by allowing his department to dispose of various wharf facilities which no longer fit the economic and trading pattern formerly prevalent along the British Columbia coast. In other words, today motor connections and the ramp loading of cars have become a major factor and wharf facilities built on piles are becoming less and less important. In the case of these unnecessary works the people of the west coast have been most co-operative. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate gets up and catalogues the vast requirements of the people of his riding, leaving me to wonder what he did for them while he was a minister of the crown. In this case we have works going forward which have been contributed to in a major way by the people surrendering works of a nature not now required.
Quite aside from the commercial necessity, we have a requirement today for shelter for small craft. Today on a week end between 40,000 and 45,000 small craft ply the inner waters of the strait of Georgia and Malaspina strait, and only in very rare cases have we ever recognized our responsibility to provide shelter to which these thousands of craft can run in the event of a sudden squall. Unless steps are taken now, one of these days we are going to be faced with a tragedy.
I would ask the minister to think about this matter very seriously. I would point
fMr. Payne.]

out that the difficulty of proving the need for shelters along the long exposed coast line of the Sechelt peninsula is such that it is almost impossible to surmount. The historic requirements of the department are that first of all you must show economic need. This is certainly putting the cart before the horse. Nobody can make use of a shelter along that coast line unless shelter exists and it. is impossible to try to establish in a statistical way a situation that cannot develop until the much needed shelter is provided. Such statistics cannot be supplied to anyone until shelter is provided.
In a not too critical way, I hope, I say, as a British Columbian who feels a responsibility to those who ply the waters of the Pacific and the sheltered waters of our inland canals, that I believe that greater emphasis and attention must be placed on the needs of the west coast. Surely a great maritime province such as British Columbia with its apparent needs is justified in expecting an amount to be provided for such services far greater in ratio than that which is before us in the estimates this year.
My criticisms and my suggestions in this connection are not directed against the minister in his capacity as Minister of Public Works. This pattern is a historic one. The same recognition of the need of Canada's west coast has been shown by past ministers over many years. All I am asking today is that the matter be looked at closely and put in its proper perspective.
Before taking my seat, I should like to thank the department again for its continuing program with respect to the building of a sea wall around the historic area of Stanley park. I should also like to make one suggestion. Much of the harbour of Vancouver is taken up by what is known as the north shore area, which is the southern boundary of my beautiful riding. I would urge that some consideration be given to establishing a continuing program, as has been done in the case of Stanley park, whereby the approaches to Canada's western gateway may at long last have the sea wall which they so badly need.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to make a few observations. First of all, I wish to refer to the surface of the wharf at Crawford Bay. The wharf is a rock-filled crib structure that cost around $30,000 and it is an excellent wharf. There is an earth covering over the rock fill and owing to large trucks using the wharf for the unloading of logs and so on the surface has been very much

cut up and has been somewhat neglected until recently. The minister's department is going to look into the matter and improve the surface at the first opportunity.
I suggest that the department investigate the possibility of providing an asphalt surface like that at the Kaslo wharf. It makes an excellent surface for these rock-filled, earth-topped wharves. I am not suggesting any large expenditure but I do ask the department, because of the requests of a number of residents, to look into that question. It makes an excellent launching ramp for small craft belonging to local people and for the many tourists who use the highway which passes nearby.
I want to say that the residents of Kootenay Bay are delighted to know that the department intends to build a launching ramp or proper launching facilities there because there is an increasing number of people coming from the United States particularly who will use these launching facilities and they will also serve the local people.
The people of Slocan city have requested for a couple years the consideration of the building of launching facilities there. I understand the policy of the department is that these launching facilities are provided where the major industry is catering to tourists. I would ask them to look into that question again because the number of tourists who stay in that small city is increasing every year. It is a historical place, an old mining community that was very much larger at one time than it is today. It was at one time the smallest city in North America having a population of about 272 persons in an area a mile square. It is in a most attractive spot at the south end of Slocan lake, with an excellent beach three quarters of a mile long fronting this small city, which of course attracts tourists there in increasing numbers.
I come to one other question, and I hope the minister does not think I am at all avaricious. I am just putting forward the views of my constituents. The Nakusp launch club, supported by the chamber of commerce and other organizations, asked the minister to give reconsideration to the necessity for a small breakwater behind which United States small craft can shelter. Last year, we had about 125 of these small craft come up. I just got word today of about 20 being there. Under storm conditions, it is very difficult for them to find satisfactory shelter. Some of these craft are too large to beach. Some of them are quite expensive cruisers, and are quite elaborate. They come from as far south as Portland, being portaged around the Grand Coulee dam and the Bonneville dam on huge trucks or lowboys, as 90205-6-4111
Supply-Public Works
I think the term is. Since the people of the United States have discovered this paradise in which we live, they are coming in increasing numbers.
I have a suggestion to make. I am under the impression, and I know something about the cost of piling and logs, that the department has, on occasion, possibly paid an unnecessarily high price for piling and logs required for the foundations for breakwaters and that sort ol thing. Since the war all the lumber companies have been very busy. These small orders have been somewhat of a nuisance to the larger operators. There would be possibly two or three people who would bid on these contracts for piling and logs under these circumstances and because the order is small and a particular effort is required to get these materials out, the prices have been somewhat high. I do suggest consideration be given to calling for tenders for these piles and logs that are required in the construction of wharves during the winter when there are many unemployed men with families who would be very pleased indeed to undertake this work at a reasonable cost. I make that as a suggestion in respect of this breakwater.
I am of the opinion that this is a very necessary breakwater because Nakusp is the main port on the Arrow lakes, in fact it is the capital of the Arrow lakes. These boats usually come up from as far south as Portland and stay there overnight before continuing their journey to Revelstoke. I have been rather astounded at the estimated cost of this work as given by the minister's officials. I know something about the construction of these facilities. I believe the high estimated cost is due to the cost of the raw materials. The piledrivers are there and the driving of the piles would not occupy more than a day. The other facilities needed for this kind of work are there, too. I suggest that with some co-operation with this launch club and the local organizations, this breakwater could be built at about half the cost of the estimate provided by the minister when the matter last received consideration. I just put forward that suggestion.
I want to say a word or two about Duncan river.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt the hon. member for Kootenay West, but there was some suggestion that we might be able to get through some of these items by six o'clock. The hon. member for Kootenay West often drops in to see me. Could he outline the details of some of these projects to me during a private visit? I do not want to interfere in any way with the hon. member in presenting his comments, but it would

Supply-Public Works
be appreciated if we could get through some of these items. We have had three hard days so far.

I am in a very co-operative mood. I was going to say a few words about Duncan river and the dredging of the Arrow lakes. However, I shall accept the minister's suggestion and call on him at the first opportunity that is convenient to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Thank you very much.

I do want to underline, if I may, the remarks made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano with regard to the great need which exists for boat shelters. I expect this need is more prevalent in the lower coastal area because of the population than it is in some of the outlying regions. I spent almost a year travelling up and down the coast by small craft, and know from personal experience the need that exists for these breakwaters and shelters.
At this stage, I would not want to become involved in any difference of opinion which might arise between the hon. member for Coast-Capilano and some hon. members from Newfoundland about the relative importance of each coast or the different amounts of money that are assigned to each coast. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that on a number of occasions I have expressed similar thoughts with regard to fisheries and, on another occasion, with regard to the subsidies for shipping and transportation. I pointed out the disparity that exists between the two coasts.
Over the last two years there has been some work developing on the northern coast of the Queen Charlotte islands at Wiah point or Seven Mile point. Perhaps the minister could give us an account of this work, if he would. I am sure it would be very brief. Before the minister replies, I should point out for the benefit of the hon. member for Kootenay West who raised the question of the initial estimates of such projects, that the initial estimate of the Wiah point project was greatly in excess of what it actually cost to do the dredging and the breakwater work that was necessary. Some thoughts have been expressed to the effect that it is sometimes the policy of a minister who does not want to say no to a particular project and be accused of being unfair to one part of the country as compared with another, to take the initial estimated cost and double or treble it, then say it is far too costly to do that this year. I do not say this Minister of Public Works does that.
However, as I say, I have met this situation with regard to Wiah point. The initial estimates were far in excess of the actual cost. I am sure the minister of highways for

British Columbia sometimes does this overestimating in order to curtail argument and pressure from groups in the community in relation to proceeding with particular road projects. We have seen, on a couple of occasions, that the final cost was less than the initial estimated cost, which seems to be a bit difficult to understand.
I wonder, too, if the minister would give us an account of what is taking place with regard to the dredging of Metlakatla bar, just outside Prince Rupert. I have exchanged a lot of correspondence with the department. Once they said yes; at another stage they said no, then yes, and then the captain of the dredge was involved in the argument, too. The last information I received was to the effect there was going to be some dredging at Metlakatla bar. I wonder if the minister could give us an indication of what is happening in connection with those two items.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In reply to the hon. member for Skeena, I would say he is quite right. This work is being planned and I understand we hope to get it under way very shortly.

I just want to make a few brief comments on the remarks made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. I do not want to become embroiled in any argument as to the relative importance of the Vancouver coast and the Newfoundland coast. I do not know anything about the coast of British Columbia. I therefore do not propose to have anything at all to say about it. If there are needs on the British Columbia coast, I would think that those who are representing British Columbia here in the House of Commons will be well able to speak for the constituencies who sent them here. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that nobody will ever hear from me any complaints about any hon. member talking too long in order to place before parliament the needs of the area which he represents. I am just a little bit annoyed that anyone should take occasion to object to my representing the area from which I come. I do not know the length of the Vancouver coast or how many projects are required. I have no doubt the hon. gentleman has requirements and I have no doubt that he does a good job of placing those requirements before the minister. However, I should like to do exactly the same thing.
In my province we need a large number of marine works. I come from an island where the coast line is 6,000 miles long, and where along that coast line there are 1,200 small settlements; to that figure you will have to add another 3,000 miles for the coast line of Labrador. Surely on the coast line it is to be expected that there would be a

great need for marine construction. True it is that in the early thirties many of the marine works that were built along the coast of Newfoundland were destroyed and the government of the day was unable to replace them. However, coming into the mid 40's and well before Newfoundland came into confederation in 1949, a number of these marine works were replaced. From 1949 until the present government came into office a good deal was done to provide the needed marine works. Let us be fair about this matter. Since 1957, the present minister and his predecessor have done exactly the same thing. But because all this has been done I see no reason why there should be any objection to explaining to the minister what further things are required. The Newfoundlanders who sit in this House of Commons listen for days and days to members from western Canada talk about agricultural products, but you never here any complaint from Newfoundlanders, and I am certainly not going to complain. They have their case to place before parliament and they have a right to do so. I claim the right to do exactly the same thing. I may not talk about exactly the same problems that exist in British Columbia or the prairies. Maybe in the case of Newfoundland we are talking about fish; in the case of the prairies we are talking about wheat. However, they are all products of Canada. Let me say to some of the western members that you cannot live by bread alone.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 355 carry?

Before it carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to relate to the minister a couple of following thoughts I have or rather thoughts following upon what I had originally said about the need for breakwaters and the like. I have had correspondence over this matter with the department and with the minister and have had discussions with them for some time. The department and the minister's officials have been kind enough to conduct in some instances, surveys and investigations of the requests and in others they have not yet quite reached that stage. However, I would point out that the north coastal area is to a great extent, at least on the coastal part, dependent upon the fishing industry. The north coastal part is not so well protected as is that area between the mainland and Vancouver island on the lower coastal part.
Throughout the entire Queen Charlotte islands and the entire north coastal area we are at the complete mercy of the Pacific winds and storms from the southeast in the fall and winter months and it gets extremely
Supply-Public Works
dangerous to go fishing on many occasions, with no shelter in sight. This Wiah Point that we mentioned earlier was a case in point of being the only possible place on the whole north coast of the Queen Charlotte islands that could be developed into some sort of haven for the fishing fleet that fish out of there. Some work was done and that is most helpful and most appreciated by the trawlers that work off the north island and Seven Mile, Masset inlet and the parts along the north coast of the Queen Charlotte islands.
In the middle of the Queen Charlotte islands, on Skidegate inlet there is another group of settlements containing a fairly large number of people who are fishermen with rather expensive boats. This is near Queen Charlotte city or Skidegate. There are a dock and two floats there, but generally the boats are at the complete mercy of any storms that blow up anywhere along the north coast. There is no shelter whatsoever and they are moored out in the bay and Skidegate inlet. The people have been complaining and asking for and insisting upon a breakwater to be established there-a rock filled breakwater-for many years now but so far no breakwater exists; and any time that a storm blows up or storm warnings are up those individuals who have boats out in the inlet have to get up, whether it is in the middle of the night, middle of the morning or any other time or off fishing days and row out to the boats, unmoor them and move away down the inlet in order to gain some protection from the winds that blow up there almost overnight in the fall and in the winter parts of the year.
This is an extremely important matter. I wish the minister would undertake to delve into this particular question of a breakwater at Skidegate. When he is doing this, I wish he would pay less attention to the question of cost as it relates to the number of people who might use it. The lives of individuals are involved as well as the value of their ships just as is the case at another community, namely Port Simpson just north of Prince Rupert. The minister's department made some investigations there. They came back with the answer that it would cost too much to provide the breakwater facilities; that there were not enough people here with boats of enough value that would get enough benefit out of the breakwater even if we were to put it in, but it cost too much anyhow. To look purely and simply at the dollars and cents end of it and to establish some arbitrary rule, if that is what is done, about whether or not a breakwater, a dock, or some other safety device of that nature is established I think is the wrong thing to do.

Supply-Public Works
Port Simpson, for instance is an Indian village and I think it will remain for some time at generally the present level of population and that the increase will come from an increase in the birth rate. It will remain for some period of time, I would think, in relatively the same economic position, with relatively the same number of boats and the same number of people operating them, with gradual increases arising out of population alone or perhaps intermarriage into the bands. To me this means that for a long period of time to come those people are going to be denied the right to safety and a safe mooring place behind a breakwater because it is considered to be uneconomic by the department.
I could mention a number of other places on the north coast that are in the same position. The minister I am sure has under consideration one that immediately comes to mind at Hartley Bay where a great need also exists for a breakwater. This is also an Indian village and it is also going to remain in relatively the same position economically and with respect to population for quite a number of years to come.
Without going into all of these other requirements and needs by name at this time, I just wanted to use these one or two instances in order to point out to the minister and I think in a number of cases, far too much consideration or almost exclusive consideration appears to have been given-or at least this is the feeling that the people in those communities have-to the question of cost and that the sole concern is dollars and cents related to the number of people who might be using that particular facility. When the lives of individuals are involved and when their investment in boats, fishing equipment and gear is involved, I think if this is the criterion the department uses, it is an incorrect one.
I wonder whether the minister would also say what is happening with respect to the requests of people at Oona River who wanted to participate jointly with the department in some work at that particular community by supplying labour and the like if the department would supply some additional equipment and money in order to establish facilities there. I would like the minister to give an account of what is happening there.
I was not able to be in the chamber earlier, unfortunately, and perhaps at that time the minister dealt with the matter raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East yesterday, namely the situation at San Juan in which the minister had quite a bit of interest prior to the by-elections and indicated to the house, as I read his words, that all that was necessary was to elect the Conservative candidate for Esquimalt-Saanich and the breakwater

would be built overnight. If the minister has already dealt with that matter and it is on Hansard, perhaps he will let me know and I will find it. If he has not, perhaps he will deal with this particular point.
Are those all the afterthoughts the hon. member has?
I beg your pardon?
The hon. member made one speech and then said, "I have some afterthoughts". I wondered whether he had any more afterthoughts.

If my hon. friend invites me, I will be glad to accept the invitation. What I said was not that these were afterthoughts, but thoughts which I hoped to express after I received a reply from the minister on the question of Wiah point and Metlakatla bay. Also, I saw the hon. member for Humber-St. George's rising at the same time as myself and I thought perhaps he wanted to deal with the question of the relative treatment of the east and west coasts. I certainly did not want to take up all the time and prevent him having an opportunity of taking part in the debate.
I know the Minister of Veterans Affairs has accused me of doing this before, that is, preventing hon. members like my hon. friend from Vancouver South having a say in this house. That is a pretty sad situation. However, I may be able to follow the invitation of the hon. member after the minister has replied to the questions I have asked.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

No, Mr. Chairman. I think this question of San Juan is one in which we should perhaps get involved a little more, because the minister with a smirk on his face the other day when questions were asked about this, obviously meant-and in fact almost said it-that he had been in touch with an individual who was the reeve of Saanich. When he was asked a question a couple of days later he qualified that and said this was the individual who would be the next member

of parliament representing the constituency of Esquimalt-Saanich; and he was.
This is what happened, and there is no doubt at all that the statements of the minister were used to advantage in that particular constituency. Perhaps anyone who had been in the same position would have used them in the same way. I think perhaps all candidates take advantage of using government information of this kind, if they can, in order to get a few votes. The unfortunate thing that develops out of this practice is that such projects and matters are purely and simply vote-getters and do not mean anything in so far as concrete action is concerned.
One would not want to see this particular request carried on year after year after year waiting for other elections and by-elections for the minister to consider it. I know how long these things carry on and how much delay takes place in giving them what is known as proper consideration. I know how many petitions have to be signed, letters written, requests made, resolutions passed and everything else before action is taken. Esquimalt-Saanich is not my constituency and I only raise this matter as an incidental in this discussion because I have asked questions about it before.
I have been in that part of the country. The hon. member for Vancouver East dealt with the subject last evening. Perhaps the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich at some time intends to ask the minister about this particular item or perhaps he has already done so. Perhaps the hon. member has been in touch with the minister and may want to deal with it further.
I suppose the minister has an excuse if this is not contained in the estimates now before us, because they were prepared long before the by-election was called. The minister has that excuse, perhaps, if he wants to use that sort of excuse. However, there are supplementary estimates which we will also be dealing with, and I notice it is not included in there either. I only want to say that I hope this is not one of those items which drags on and on and on, year after year continually being given consideration, with no action being taken.
This is what happens to requests for so many projects of a similar nature. I have mentioned a couple of them already. I have mentioned the one at Port Simpson and the one at Skidegate. The projects I have mentioned would be of great benefit to the people there, just the same as the projects mentioned by the hon. member from Coast-Capilano would be of benefit to the people of that area.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier asked some questions yesterday and the answers, as I have them seriatim, are as follows:
Dorion, Quebec. No steps are being taken to develop a major harbour at Dorion.
Cornwall, Ontario. Engineering investigations have been carried out under the advance planning program of the Department of Public Works to prepare an over-all plan with cost estimates for a harbour development to handle both bulk and package freight. Any development undertaken is to proceed in stages, with only a modest outlay in the first instance, with further stages to depend upon the growth traffic.
A single berth wharf, 400 feet long, providing for ships with a 21-foot draft, but expandable both as to depth and length of face, is to be constructed this fiscal year. Tenders are expected to be advertised next week.
Morrisburg, Ontario. There is not now sufficient basis to warrant a major deep water harbour development at this place. Morrisburg will rapidly increase in importance as a tourist centre and, consequently, there was a reasonable case for the provision of tourist wharfage facilities.
An L-shaped timber cribwork and span structure, 180 feet by 16 feet, is presently under construction. This wharf is nearing completion and the contract price was $22,280.
Prescott, Ontario:
(a)	A deep water facility is not warranted at Prescott;
(b)	There are the Johnston national harbours board deep water wharfage facilities on the west side of the elevator slip which can be utilized for general cargo, provided that a transit shed facility is installed;
(c)	The Department of Public Works has constructed such a transit shed about 60 by 200 feet on the national harbours board wharf, west of the elevator slip; this shed is being administered by the national harbours board.
The approximate cost of this shed was $58,000.
At Brockville, Ontario, no steps are being taken to construct deep water harbour facilities at Brockville until such time as there

Supply-Public Works
are firm indications of the volume and nature of traffic which would use the harbour.
At Oshawa, Ontario, a wharf structure, 500 feet long is to be constructed on the eastern side of the harbour to provide additional berthing. The cost of this construction will approach one half million dollars.

speechtext: I thank the minister. There was another question which I put, namely, why the construction work would not begin until the month of August, as stated in the local press.

357. Remedial works where damages are caused by, or endanger, navigation or federal government structures, $800,000.

I have asked the minister time and time again, and I ask him again today, what can we expect from the department by way of protection wharves. I have stated that before Mr. Winters became minister of public works successive ministers in both Conservative and Liberal governments had always recognized a certain responsibility for the provision of protection wharves along navigable rivers. When Mr. Winters took over it was decided that "navigable" should be construed as "navigated" and from that time ministers of public works have refused to accept responsibility along navigable rivers.
I have written to the minister stating my case. I have told him that while Ottawa was saying, "it is not our responsibility", Quebec was saying that it was the responsibility of Ottawa because damage was occurring along navigable rivers, not navigated rivers. For this reason I have from time to time asked the minister why the federal and the provincial authorities should not get together to decide exactly who is responsible in these cases. It is claimed that erosion by waters in the spring is an act of God. But we also suffer from the effects of erosion every Sunday because the numerous dams on the Gatineau and Ottawa rivers are opened Saturday. Then the water rises and it goes into the land affecting the land belonging to farmers along the river. They close again on Saturday night so that they can get water for power, and the water goes down. This certainly cannot be called an act of God. It is an act of man. We should like to know definitely who is responsible for these things.

The minister wrote me a letter two and a half pages long but I cannot accept it as clearing up the situation perfectly. The only way in which we could have a clear answer would be for the federal and provincial authorities to get together and accept the joint responsibility they might have, together with their individual responsibilities. I should like to hear from the minister whether or not he intends to submit the problem to the provincial authorities to see what can be done.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall the item
carry?

I should like to have an answer from the minister. I know that in the letter he sent me he does not admit he is obliged to. I understand that he is not forced to take action but if he wishes to clear up this matter this would be a way of doing so. The minister will have to do so one way or the other-either he or his successor. If this matter were cleared up we should know where to strike when we want to get something done. Farmers in a great many places in my riding along the Ottawa river have been affected including those at Gatineau Point, Templeton, Masson and Buckingham. They have been affected in all parts, and I know this situation exists not only along the Ottawa river and the Gatineau river but along many other rivers in Canada. The minister should give us the necessary answer so that we might know who is responsible and where we should strike if we need help in these matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall the item
carry?
I am not ready to let it carry in this way. I think the minister should at least give the committee an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The answer is fully set out, with clarity and detail, in the long letter which took hours and hours of preparation so that the hon. member for Hull might be able to understand. There is no change in government policy. I had hoped the hon. member would understand the letter. If he does not, I shall be glad if he will come to my office and I will go over it point by point.
Carried.

I am not ready to accept it that way. The minister seems to have made up his mind that the answer he gave was satisfactory. I know that the provincial authorities say it was not so. They claim this is the responsibility of the federal government. The federal government denies this. How can we get a clear-cut answer with regard to this matter? Either we shall have

to send cases to the supreme court in order to have a ruling or the two parties must get together to decide. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The legislative items for Monday and Tuesday are 10 in number. The order in which they will be considered is as follows: No. 1, a bill to amend the Criminal Code; No. 2, Bill No. C-109, with regard to the Financial Administration Act; No. 3, Bill No. S-28, with regard to the Trust Companies Act; No. 4, Bill No. S-29, with regard to the Loan Companies Act; No. 5, Bill No. S-24, with regard to the Government Property Traffic Act. No. 6 will be the resolution in my name, followed immediately by consideration in committee of the whole of Bill

Business of the House
No. C-101, to amend the War Veterans' Allowance Act. No. 7 will be Bill No. C-108, concerning the Export Credits Insurance Act. No. 8 will be a bill to amend the Energy Board Act. It depends on the progress made on Monday and Tuesday on these legislative items. Thursday and Friday will be given over to the budget debate and Saturday will be devoted to estimates.
I think it is a little early to predict the estimates that may be taken up next week. We have now completed nine departments, we have dealt partially with four others. Two are in committee. Therefore there are not very many left but the house will have to determine how rapidly it would like to progress with the estimates.
